title: ICU Integration: Cardiac Arrest, Sedation, Nutrition & Recovery
note: Set 9: Learn chapters (ICU Integration: Cardiac Arrest, Sedation, Nutrition & Recovery notes, structured for easy reading), learning outcomes, landmark trials and a linked reading list. Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content to follow.

items.title: 1. A conceptual framework: why ICU integration requires different reasoning
items.los: Integrates the outcomes in this set
items.body:
- Intensive care medicine is not simply the sum of separate organ-support techniques.

In a critically ill patient, treatment for one system affects several others:

- Sedative drugs lower blood pressure and alter delirium risk.
- Positive-pressure ventilation can reduce venous return.
- Enteral feed increases glucose and insulin demand.
- Renal or hepatic failure changes drug exposure.
- The goals of organ support may change when recovery becomes unlikely.

- A candidate approaching independent specialist practice should be able to explain which problem matters most now, why a proposed intervention is likely to help, what harm it could cause, and what finding would make them change the plan.

This set begins with the most time-critical example—cardiac arrest—then follows the patient through post-arrest organ support, analgesia/sedation, nutrition and catabolic stress, severity assessment, prolonged recovery and decisions about limits of treatment. The same practical cycle recurs throughout:

**Recognise deterioration → identify a plausible mechanism → institute immediate stabilisation → test the mechanism → deliver definitive treatment → reassess response and complications → redefine goals.**

Although a cardiac-arrest algorithm is a useful cognitive aid, it does not remove the need to reason about the cause. Similarly, a sedation target, protein prescription, APACHE score or “full escalation” label is meaningful only if it is interpreted in the patient’s specific clinical circumstances.

items.title: 2. The physiology and aetiology of perioperative cardiac arrest
items.body:
## 2.1 Why arrest during anaesthesia differs from arrest on the ward

- Anaesthesia-associated collapse is usually witnessed, monitored, occurs in a controlled environment with an immediately accessible airway and intravenous access, and frequently has a reversible iatrogenic, physiological or procedural cause.
- The anaesthetist can often identify a changing capnogram, arterial waveform, ECG, airway pressure, oxygen saturation or surgical event before pulselessness.
- That creates an opportunity to interrupt progression from compensated shock to profound low-flow and no-flow states.
- The 2025 perioperative resuscitation (PeRLS) update emphasises rapid, cause-directed action alongside conventional high-quality resuscitation [R04].

Arrest mechanisms can be understood as sudden failure of one or more determinants of forward blood flow and oxygen delivery:

- **Preload failure:** major haemorrhage, venodilatation from induction, severe dehydration, aortocaval compression, impaired venous return from tension pneumothorax or severe auto-PEEP.
- **Pump failure:** myocardial infarction/ischaemia, profound bradyarrhythmia, ventricular tachyarrhythmia, severe cardiomyopathy, myocardial depression from drugs or hypoxia, acute right-ventricular failure.
- **Mechanical obstruction:** tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolism, gas embolism, severe dynamic hyperinflation or major outflow obstruction.
- **Vascular-tone failure:** anaphylaxis, high neuraxial blockade, profound sympathectomy, severe sepsis or other vasoplegia.
- **Primary hypoxaemia or ventilation failure:** lost/displaced airway, failed oxygen supply, ventilator disconnection, oesophageal intubation, aspiration, severe bronchospasm, one-lung ventilation mishap or high airway pressure.
- **Metabolic/toxic causes:** severe potassium or calcium disturbance, local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), profound acid–base derangement, drug overdose, malignant hyperthermia and hypothermia.

- In an anaesthetised patient without an arterial line, a falling ETCO₂ is not itself proof of arrest.
- It is an early sign of reduced pulmonary blood flow or increased dead space; verify an arterial pulse/trace and ECG promptly, while treating the likely cause.
- Abrupt disappearance of ETCO₂ may also represent disconnection or displacement.
- When the patient is ventilated and the ECG still shows an organised rhythm, a nearly absent arterial trace strongly supports pulseless electrical activity (PEA).

- Recognising impending cardiovascular collapse requires comparing the monitor channels, not one isolated number.
- In an intubated patient at constant minute ventilation, end-tidal CO₂ approximates pulmonary perfusion as well as CO₂ production: a rapid fall from 35 to 12 mmHg during acute hypotension supports severe reduction in pulmonary blood flow, but the causes include a major pulmonary embolus, haemorrhage, gas embolism, severe myocardial failure and true arrest.
- A capnogram that disappears completely without a matching ECG or arterial change suggests circuit disconnection, oesophageal displacement or sampling failure.
- Check the actual waveform and its trend, the ECG, an arterial tracing if present, pulse and the operation in progress.
- Do not diagnose or terminate cardiac arrest solely using ETCO₂.

- The distinction between profound hypotension and pulseless electrical activity is particularly important during anaesthesia.
- A narrow pulse pressure with a weak but reproducible arterial waveform indicates some forward flow and deserves immediate treatment of the cause before deterioration into arrest.
- An organised ECG without demonstrable flow after a prompt assessment is PEA: begin compressions and treat the precipitant.
- Point-of-care ultrasound can show whether the left ventricle is contracting but must never create prolonged compression pauses.
- Ventricular movement with no useful systemic output does not rule out the need for CPR.

## 2.2 Anticipating arrest before induction

- The highest-risk phases are not all equivalent.
- At induction, loss of sympathetic tone, decreased systemic vascular resistance (SVR), impaired contractility, apnea and the shift from spontaneous to positive-pressure breathing can trigger collapse in patients dependent on endogenous catecholamines or venous return.
- During a procedure, the trigger may be local anaesthetic injection, insufflation, surgical haemorrhage, clamp manipulation, cement implantation, embolisation, vagal stimulation or a rapid transfusion reaction.
- Emergence introduces the risks of obstruction, hypoxaemia, aspiration, arrhythmia and rapid haemodynamic fluctuations.

- For a patient with severe aortic stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, pericardial tamponade, advanced shock or ongoing haemorrhage, prevention means more than choosing an induction drug.
- Plan vascular access and vasoactive rescue, have blood available, consider invasive arterial monitoring before induction if it does not create harmful delay, minimise unnecessary fasting or fluid loss, coordinate procedural timing and agree on a rescue plan.
- In haemorrhagic shock, controlling bleeding may be more important than a “smooth” induction; in severe pulmonary hypertension, avoiding hypoxia, acidosis and abrupt systemic hypotension may be lifesaving.

## 2.3 Differential diagnosis by the monitor pattern

| **Early observation** | **Likely physiology** | **Key immediate checks and actions** |
|---|---|---|
| Sudden fall in ETCO₂, arterial BP collapse, airway pressures unchanged | Abrupt fall in pulmonary blood flow: PE, gas embolus, arrest, major bleeding | Confirm pulse/arterial trace; correlate with procedure; examine RV by echo if immediately available; stop source and initiate CPR if pulseless |
| High airway pressure, obstructive expiratory flow, falling BP | Tension pneumothorax, bronchospasm, kink/occlusion, auto-PEEP | Disconnect briefly if dynamic hyperinflation suspected; assess tube and breath sounds; ultrasound; immediate thoracic decompression when tension suspected |
| Hypotension with bronchospasm, rash or angio-oedema | Perioperative anaphylaxis | Stop suspected exposure, 100% O₂, IV adrenaline and fluid; summon help; continue escalation per ANZAAG/ANZCOR |
| Severe bradycardia after spinal/epidural or surgical traction | High neuraxial block, vagal reflex, underfilled circulation | Stop stimulus; assess block/ventilation/preload; atropine or adrenaline as appropriate; rapid support if pulseless |
| Widened QRS, sine wave, or ventricular arrhythmia after transfusion/renal failure | Hyperkalaemia, other metabolic disturbance | ECG and rapid blood gas; IV calcium for membrane stabilisation, potassium-shifting/removal therapy; ALS if arrest |
| Sudden ST change, acute LV failure, VT/VF | Ischaemia/infarction, severe haemodynamic demand, coronary or air embolism | Defibrillate if pulseless shockable; restore coronary perfusion; obtain echo and coronary input after ROSC |

A rapid ultrasound examination can help identify tamponade, major RV dilatation, profound LV failure, hypovolaemia or pneumothorax. **Do not allow image acquisition to interrupt effective compressions:** obtain views during a planned rhythm-check pause or while another operator maintains CPR.

items.title: 3. Adult advanced life support: mechanism, sequence and decisions
items.body:
## 3.1 What actually maintains perfusion during cardiac arrest

- Coronary perfusion during CPR depends chiefly on the aortic-to-right-atrial pressure difference during decompression.
- Good compressions build aortic diastolic pressure and maintain a limited but potentially adequate flow to myocardium and brain; allowing full recoil prevents persistent intrathoracic pressure and facilitates venous return.
- Interruptions dissipate coronary perfusion pressure, meaning subsequent compressions must rebuild it.
- Defibrillation terminates chaotic electrical activity but does not itself create sustained myocardial perfusion unless the myocardium is capable of organised contraction.

- For adults, compress the lower half of the sternum at **100–120/min**, depth **5–6 cm**, with full recoil and minimal interruptions.
- Switch compressors approximately every 2 minutes.
- Without an advanced airway, use **30 compressions to 2 breaths**; with an advanced airway, continue compressions and deliver around **10 breaths/min**, avoiding hyperventilation.
- Apply 100% oxygen initially and verify airway placement with continuous waveform capnography.
- Excessive ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return and may worsen cerebral perfusion [R01–R03].

## 3.2 The ANZCOR rhythm-based approach

**Shockable rhythms—VF and pulseless VT:**

- Start CPR, attach pads, charge while compressions continue and deliver a biphasic shock (ANZCOR default **200 J**, or evidence-supported manufacturer setting; escalate if unsuccessful).
- Resume compressions immediately for approximately 2 minutes without unnecessary pulse checks.
- After the **second unsuccessful shock**, give **adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO**, then repeat approximately every **4 minutes** (every second loop).
- After the **third shock**, give **amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO**; if persistent, **150 mg after the fifth shock** may be considered.
- Lignocaine **1 mg/kg**, followed if needed by **0.5 mg/kg**, is an alternative; do not routinely combine antiarrhythmics.
- Throughout, correct reversible causes [R01, R02].

**Non-shockable rhythms—PEA and asystole:**

- Start high-quality CPR immediately and administer **adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO as soon as feasible**, repeating every second loop.
- Search actively for reversible causes.
- Shock delivery is not indicated unless a shockable rhythm develops.
- Distinguish fine VF from asystole using appropriate lead/pad selection and gain, but do not prolong a pause attempting to interpret the rhythm.

**Medication details:**

- IV access is preferred; use IO if IV cannot be established rapidly.
- Give a flush to deliver central circulation.
- Routine calcium, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium, atropine or high-dose adrenaline do **not** improve survival in undifferentiated arrest and are reserved for a specific cause or indication.
- Calcium is appropriate for hyperkalaemic arrest or significant hypocalcaemia; bicarbonate may be appropriate for severe hyperkalaemia or sodium-channel blockade, not simply because an arrest blood gas is acidotic.
- Vasopressin is not a routine substitute for adrenaline.
- The 2025 CoSTR-based ANZCOR medication update retains these principles [R02].

- Critically evaluating resuscitation means separating interventions with compelling patient-centred benefit from those that improve an intermediate endpoint or remain uncertain.
- The strongest reproducible evidence supports early recognition, immediately effective compressions, minimal no-flow time and early defibrillation of VF/pVT.
- Adrenaline increases the chance of return of spontaneous circulation and survival to hospital admission, but the PARAMEDIC2 randomised trial in out-of-hospital arrest found only a small increase in 30-day survival (3.2% versus 2.4%) and did not establish an improvement in favourable neurological outcome.
- It is therefore reasonable to follow ANZCOR's drug algorithm while explaining that reversal of the precipitating cause, rather than drug escalation alone, drives meaningful recovery [R26].

- Airway intervention is also a balancing decision.
- Early tracheal intubation by a skilled anaesthetist can control ventilation, prevent gastric insufflation and permit continuous compressions, but a prolonged attempt can interrupt oxygenation or defibrillation.
- In AIRWAYS-2, a large prehospital randomised study, functional outcome was not improved by assigning a supraglottic airway rather than tracheal intubation (6.4% versus 6.8% favourable functional outcome); this does not imply equivalence in anaesthetised operating-theatre patients with different operator expertise.
- Deliver oxygen and capnography reliably using whichever technique can be achieved without delaying CPR [R31].

- Mechanical chest compression devices are not a routine replacement for skilled manual CPR.
- They can facilitate high-quality compression during transport, angiography or prolonged resuscitation where manual CPR is impractical or unsafe, but require training, careful placement and interruption minimisation.
- Extracorporeal CPR restores oxygenation and blood flow in selected refractory arrests, but evidence is heterogeneous: the INCEPTION randomised trial found favourable neurological survival at 30 days of 20% with ECPR versus 16% with conventional CPR (not statistically significant), whereas selected high-performing programmes have sometimes reported better results.
- For a witnessed arrest with a reversible lesion, short low-flow time, immediate specialist capability and acceptable premorbid function, early referral may be appropriate; it is not an evidence-based default for every refractory PEA [R32].

- Arrest termination cannot be reduced to a single fixed duration, ETCO₂ threshold, age or initial rhythm.
- Consider scene and procedure, periods without flow, whether high-quality CPR is possible, persistent reversible pathology, available surgical or ECPR rescue, response to treatment, comorbidity, known wishes and team consensus.
- Hypothermia, some toxic exposures, pulmonary embolism and other correctable causes may justify prolonged efforts.
- Document the clinical reasoning and family communication without making early neurological predictions from a low-flow examination.

## 3.3 When ordinary algorithms need modification

A witnessed, continuously monitored VF/pVT arrest with a defibrillator immediately available may justify **up to three stacked shocks**, especially in the cardiac catheter laboratory or early post-cardiac surgery. This is a narrow exception, not the standard technique for a ward or unwitnessed arrest. If ROSC does not follow the third shock promptly, start compressions [R03].

- In severe anaphylaxis, adrenaline is both the principal resuscitative drug and a treatment for the causal vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability and bronchoconstriction.
- Before complete arrest, small titrated IV boluses or infusion according to the perioperative algorithm are more appropriate than automatically giving the 1 mg cardiac-arrest dose.
- If the patient becomes pulseless, commence ALS.
- In severe hypovolaemia or ongoing uncontrolled haemorrhage, compression quality alone cannot restore effective filling: **simultaneous haemorrhage control and blood resuscitation are essential**.

- In massive pulmonary embolism, refractory PEA reflects acute RV pressure overload and loss of LV filling.
- Consider thrombolysis, catheter-directed reperfusion, surgical embolectomy or ECPR when available and appropriate.
- ANZCOR advises that after fibrinolytic treatment for strongly suspected PE arrest, extended CPR **60–90 minutes** may be considered [R03].
- In tension pneumothorax, decompress immediately and follow with thoracostomy/drain; do not defer life-saving decompression for radiographic confirmation.

## 3.4 Physiological monitoring during CPR

- Waveform capnography assists confirmation of tracheal placement, evaluation of CPR quality and detection of ROSC, although values are strongly affected by ventilation, pulmonary pathology and cause of arrest.
- An abrupt sustained increase in ETCO₂ may indicate improved cardiac output/ROSC; low ETCO₂ should prompt review of compression quality and cause but **must not be used as a sole stopping rule**.
- An existing invasive arterial trace helps detect perfusion during CPR, distinguish PEA from perfusing rhythm and guide treatment.
- A venous blood gas can identify severe hyperkalaemia and other treatable metabolic derangements; arterial oxygenation is difficult to interpret during low-flow CPR.

Do not routinely interrupt compressions for intubation, central access, arterial cannulation, echo or a transport decision. Assign simultaneous roles: team leader, compressor, airway, defibrillator, drugs/lines, cause assessment, recorder and runner. State each intervention and re-evaluate the plan at every 2-minute rhythm check.

items.title: 4. Arrest in special perioperative circumstances
items.body:
## 4.1 Post-cardiac-surgery arrest (CALS–ANZ)

- The pathophysiology differs from ordinary ward arrest because causes are often rapidly surgically reversible: tamponade from clot, major postoperative bleeding, graft or coronary ischaemia, pacing failure and tension pneumothorax.
- External compressions may damage recent surgical structures and do not effectively treat tamponade.
- The **2026 ANZCOR Guideline 11.10 endorses the Australasian CALS–ANZ pathway** [R03].

- In a witnessed monitored arrest: call the cardiac surgery/ICU team and prepare emergency re-sternotomy **within 5 minutes** by a trained team.
- For VF/pVT, attempt up to **three rapid stacked shocks**; for severe bradycardia or asystole with epicardial pacing wires, use asynchronous pacing (e.g. DOO) if appropriate.
- If a paced patient has PEA, briefly exclude hidden VF by checking the underlying rhythm.
- There may be a brief, deliberate delay of external compressions while these interventions are performed, but **do not withhold compressions while the team prepares for re-sternotomy**.
- Identify tamponade or bleeding, decompress the pericardium, perform internal massage and correct the lesion.
- Early survival may be better than in general cardiac arrest because the pathology is reversible and rescue is immediate, but this depends on a trained team and local capability.

- A practical CALS–ANZ sequence begins with recognition from the arterial waveform and ETCO₂, immediate announcement of arrest, 100% oxygen, confirmation of the airway/circuit and activation of the trained cardiac-surgical re-sternotomy team.
- During the first few seconds, distinguish shockable rhythm, severe bradycardia/asystole with pacing wires and paced PEA.
- With witnessed VF/pVT and an immediately available defibrillator, perform up to three rapid stacked shocks, reassessing promptly between attempts.
- With epicardial wires and asystole or profound bradycardia, attempt asynchronous pacing (DOO mode), ensuring the generator and connections function.
- With paced PEA, briefly suspend pacing to identify underlying VF rather than assuming the paced ECG reflects mechanical systole.
- ANZCOR permits withholding external compressions for up to 60 seconds for these initial targeted interventions, but not while an unsuccessful response or preparation for sternotomy continues [R03].

- This timing explains why the instruction is re-sternotomy within five minutes, not start considering re-sternotomy after five minutes.
- The team should prepare immediately: sterile kit, personal protection, chest reopening equipment, suction, light, internal defibrillator paddles and blood.
- A re-sternotomy-trained clinician opens the chest, removes clot, controls bleeding, assesses graft/heart function and institutes internal cardiac massage where indicated.
- Tamponade from clot may yield little accessible fluid on a conventional ultrasound view; a negative or equivocal study must not delay treatment when clinical suspicion is high.
- Sudden cessation of mediastinal drain output with cardiovascular collapse can mean clot occlusion and evolving tamponade, not cessation of bleeding.

- The haemodynamic goal is restored perfusion and correction of a mechanical or surgical lesion.
- Indiscriminate repeated large adrenaline boluses can create severe hypertension and further bleeding if spontaneous circulation returns abruptly; CALS pathways prioritise shock, pacing, reopening and directed support, with drug decisions individualised by the senior team.
- Outside the immediate post-cardiac-surgery period, or when the necessary team and resources are absent, the standard ALS framework and high-quality compressions remain paramount.
- A candidate should describe which CALS resources are actually available at their institution, rather than presume every ICU can safely undertake emergency resternotomy.

## 4.2 Arrest during pregnancy

- At approximately **20 weeks’ gestation or with a uterus palpable at/above the umbilicus**, relieve aortocaval compression by **manual left uterine displacement** while maintaining high-quality supine compressions; tilt must not compromise CPR.
- Manage airway and oxygenation early because pregnancy reduces functional residual capacity, increases oxygen consumption and complicates aspiration risk.
- The differential includes haemorrhage, amniotic fluid embolism, thromboembolism, eclampsia/intracranial catastrophe, sepsis, cardiac disease, anaphylaxis and high neuraxial blockade.
- Early senior obstetric, anaesthesia, neonatal and critical-care support is essential.
- Prepare for **resuscitative hysterotomy/perimortem caesarean delivery** when resuscitation is unsuccessful in a sufficiently advanced pregnancy; relieving aortocaval compression can improve maternal resuscitation.
- ANZCOR does not endorse a rigid single time cut-off that would supersede clinical judgement or local preparedness [R03].

- A pregnancy arrest also demands a decision about uterine emptying early in the resuscitation, not after prolonged unsuccessful CPR.
- At uterine size sufficient to compromise venous return (approximately ≥20 weeks), start manual left uterine displacement immediately while another clinician performs effective supine compressions.
- Prepare a resuscitative hysterotomy in parallel if circulation does not recover promptly; delivery may improve venous return, cardiac output and ventilation, and should not be delayed merely to transfer the patient to theatre.
- The traditional aim of commencing delivery by about four minutes and delivering by five minutes is a planning prompt rather than a guarantee of survival or an inflexible stop rule: act based on uterine size, reversibility and local expertise.
- Maternal resuscitation takes precedence; fetal survival becomes an additional consideration in viable gestations.
- Continue standard rhythm-specific ALS while obstetric and neonatal teams prepare, using pregnancy-specific treatment of eclampsia, haemorrhage, embolism or high block as appropriate.

## 4.3 Toxicology, local anaesthetic toxicity, hyperkalaemia and other specific causes

- Severe **local anaesthetic systemic toxicity** may manifest as CNS excitation, seizures, ventricular arrhythmia and cardiovascular collapse.
- Stop the local anaesthetic, treat seizures with small benzodiazepine doses, support airway and CPR, and administer **20% lipid emulsion** according to the current LAST guideline (typical initial bolus **1.5 mL/kg**, then **0.25 mL/kg/min** infusion; account for maximum volume and local protocol).
- Avoid vasopressin and large doses of adrenaline because they may impair lipid-resuscitation efficacy.
- Mechanical support may be necessary in refractory cases.

- **Hyperkalaemic arrest** requires membrane stabilisation with IV calcium plus potassium redistribution (insulin/dextrose, nebulised beta-agonist; bicarbonate in selected severe acidaemia) and definitive removal; act from ECG/clinical suspicion rather than waiting for a central-laboratory result.
- **Hypokalaemia** can cause malignant ventricular arrhythmia and requires potassium plus magnesium correction.
- **Tricyclic-antidepressant sodium-channel blockade** produces QRS widening, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia; sodium bicarbonate is cause-directed therapy.
- **Massive PE** is addressed above.
- **Hypothermic arrest** requires temperature-specific ANZCOR medication/defibrillation modifications and controlled rewarming, with extracorporeal support where available (Set 8 provides the detailed algorithm).

- For hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, the distinction between stabilising cardiac excitability, moving potassium intracellularly and removing it from the body prevents a common examination error.
- ANZCOR 2026 special-circumstances guidance specifies calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV promptly (or calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV), with repeat calcium considered if prolonged or refractory.
- It also specifies 10 units of short-acting insulin plus 25 g glucose IV, monitoring glucose carefully; sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV is recommended particularly when severe acidosis or renal failure coexists.
- Calcium and bicarbonate should not be mixed in the same line without adequate flushing because of precipitation risk.
- Refractory hyperkalaemia may require dialysis even during ongoing resuscitation.
- These are targeted measures in suspected/confirmed hyperkalaemia, not routine drugs for every cardiac arrest [R03].

- For local-anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), recognise that sudden seizures, widened QRS, dysrhythmias or cardiovascular collapse may follow inadvertent intravascular injection or rapid systemic absorption, sometimes without preceding neurological warning under general anaesthesia.
- Stop administration, summon help, oxygenate, control seizures and commence the current lipid-rescue protocol.
- Standard 20% lipid therapy begins at approximately 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min, with repeat bolus/increased infusion for persistent instability and a maximum cumulative dose according to the institutional/ASRA guideline.
- It is essential to distinguish lipid emulsion from propofol (which is not an adequate substitute); avoid vasopressin and large adrenaline doses, and consider ECPR for refractory cardiovascular toxicity.
- Keep a locally approved LAST checklist with the lipid emulsion supply; dose calculation during arrest is a human-factors hazard.

## 4.4 Deciding when to stop resuscitation

- Termination is an individual clinical decision, not an ETCO₂ threshold, drug-count, fixed time or single rhythm.
- Consider witnessed versus unwitnessed arrest, no-flow and low-flow durations, initial rhythm, physiological signs of reversibility, suspected poisoning/hypothermia/PE (where prolonged support may be justified), comorbidity, available definitive treatment, and known patient wishes or valid documented treatment limitations.
- Explain decisions, provide family support and document the reasoning.
- A newly discovered goals-of-care plan must be interpreted carefully rather than applied mechanically without establishing its applicability to the circumstances.

items.title: 5. Post-resuscitation syndrome and intensive care after ROSC
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 5.1 Why ROSC is only the beginning

- Successful restoration of a pulse does not imply restored organ function.
- Global ischaemia followed by reperfusion initiates mitochondrial injury, free-radical generation, endothelial activation, inflammatory signalling, microcirculatory dysfunction, vasoplegia and myocardial stunning.
- The major components of **post-cardiac-arrest syndrome** are global hypoxic–ischaemic brain injury, myocardial dysfunction, systemic ischaemia–reperfusion response and the original precipitating disease.
- Injury can continue for hours or days despite apparently acceptable systemic oxygen saturation and blood pressure.
- An immediate post-ROSC plan therefore addresses **oxygen delivery, ventilation, temperature, brain protection, coronary diagnosis, haemodynamics and delayed recovery** together.

- The first actions are a structured ABCDE reassessment, repeat 12-lead ECG, arterial blood gas, electrolyte/glucose/lactate measurement, bedside echocardiography and an investigation plan guided by the arrest cause.
- Confirm tube placement and investigate aspiration/pneumothorax.
- Reassess haemorrhage, fluid responsiveness, organ dysfunction and neurological signs, being aware that sedation, neuromuscular blockade, seizure, hypothermia and metabolic derangement confound neurological examination.
- Record arrest chronology and duration, defibrillations and drugs, because these matter for later interpretation but do not determine prognosis alone.

## 5.2 Haemodynamic management

- Post-arrest circulatory failure may reflect vasoplegia, transient myocardial stunning, acute coronary occlusion, ongoing bleeding, RV failure, tamponade or a combination.
- Echocardiography helps discriminate these; treating every low MAP with a fixed fluid bolus can worsen pulmonary oedema or RV distension.
- ANZCOR Guideline 11.7 suggests an **initial MAP at least 60–65 mmHg or SBP above 100 mmHg**, then individualise using prior blood pressure, coronary perfusion, urine output, lactate trend, capillary refill and neurological risk [R05].
- These are initial targets, not proof of optimal tissue perfusion.

- Use balanced crystalloid in small reassessed aliquots where fluid responsive and not overloaded.
- Noradrenaline is a reasonable first-line vasopressor for vasoplegia; add a contractility-directed inotrope when echo suggests low output rather than simply increasing SVR.
- For myocardial stunning with very low cardiac output, mixed vasoactive support or mechanical circulatory assistance may be considered in experienced centres.
- Document the physiological response rather than relying on drug dose alone.
- Lactate may rise transiently because of arrest, adrenaline and washout from ischaemic tissues; a single high lactate cannot establish persistent shock without considering its trajectory and context.

## 5.3 Oxygen, carbon dioxide and ventilation

- During CPR 100% oxygen is appropriate, but following ROSC prolonged hyperoxia may augment reperfusion injury.
- Initially use 100% until monitoring is reliable, then titrate to **SpO₂ approximately 94–98%** per ANZCOR, using ABGs to exclude occult hypoxaemia or inappropriate PaO₂.
- Aim for **normocapnia**, typically PaCO₂ around **35–45 mmHg (4.7–6.0 kPa)** unless a specific neurocritical or respiratory condition indicates otherwise.
- Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and could aggravate ischaemic injury; severe hypercapnia may increase cerebral blood volume and ICP.
- If ARDS or aspiration develops, apply lung-protective ventilation, balancing permissible CO₂ against cerebral physiology.
- Avoid excessive PEEP if it worsens preload/RV function, but do not sacrifice oxygenation.

## 5.4 Coronary reperfusion and competing diagnostic priorities

- An ECG with persistent ST elevation after ROSC warrants urgent coronary assessment/reperfusion according to an acute coronary syndrome pathway.
- In patients without ST elevation, immediate angiography is not necessarily beneficial for all comatose survivors; consider ongoing haemodynamic or electrical instability, recurrent ischaemia, clinical suspicion of coronary occlusion and alternate causes.
- Echo may show transient global dysfunction from post-arrest stunning, or focal abnormalities suggesting coronary pathology.
- Do not assume every shockable arrest was due to acute plaque rupture, or that an elevated post-arrest troponin proves it; CPR and global ischaemia can produce a rise.
- CT imaging, toxicology and sepsis workup should be targeted, not an indiscriminate investigation bundle that delays an obvious reversible cause.

A structured coronary decision after ROSC uses four questions:

- (1) is there persistent ST elevation or a convincing acute coronary occlusion pattern.
- (2) is there recurrent electrical instability.
- (3) is there cardiogenic shock or ongoing ischaemia.
- (4) is another cause more likely?

- Persistent ST elevation usually merits urgent angiography and reperfusion.
- Without ST elevation or ongoing instability, randomised trials such as COACT and TOMAHAWK did not demonstrate a routine survival benefit from immediate angiography in all comatose survivors.
- These trials are not a mandate to delay angiography in shock, recurrent VF or highly suspected acute coronary occlusion.
- A transient non-specific ST change immediately after defibrillation needs repeat ECG assessment, while echocardiography is useful for global stunning, regional dysfunction, RV strain and tamponade.
- Avoid transporting an unstable patient for low-yield testing at the expense of haemodynamic stabilisation or definitive treatment.

## 5.5 Temperature control and cerebral protection

- The pivotal modern distinction is between inducing hypothermia and actively preventing fever.
- In comatose adults after ROSC, **ANZCOR recommends active fever prevention with a temperature ≤37.5°C, maintained for at least 72 hours**; whether selected subgroups benefit from 32–34°C is uncertain [R06].
- The **TTM2** trial found no survival or functional advantage from targeting 33°C compared with targeted normothermia/fever treatment, with more haemodynamically significant arrhythmias in the hypothermia group [R07].
- This does **not** mean fever can be ignored or that all temperature control is unnecessary.

- Use a reliable central temperature measurement, antipyretics and active feedback-controlled temperature management when indicated.
- Shivering increases oxygen consumption and interferes with temperature regulation; analgesia, sedation, counterwarming and occasionally neuromuscular blockade may be needed, remembering that paralysis obscures seizures and neurological examination.
- Severe spontaneous hypothermia is a separate presentation: do not automatically warm a comatose mildly hypothermic post-arrest patient to normothermia if controlled fever prevention is already planned.

## 5.6 Seizure detection, glycaemia and neuroprognostication

- Seizures, including nonconvulsive seizures, may occur after brain injury; use EEG when there is clinical suspicion, myoclonus, unexplained coma or uncertainty about abnormal movements.
- Treat documented seizure activity rather than using prophylactic antiepileptic drugs indiscriminately.
- Check glucose frequently; ANZCOR advises treating hyperglycaemia >10 mmol/L while avoiding hypoglycaemia.
- Maintain stable sodium, potassium, temperature and perfusion.

**Prognostication is deliberately delayed and multimodal:**

- Residual sedatives, shock, organ failure, hypothermia, paralytic agents and seizures can create a falsely pessimistic bedside examination.
- A poor response immediately after ROSC or early myoclonus **does not independently prove an irreversible poor outcome**.
- At ≥72 hours after ROSC (and after drug/metabolic confounders are excluded), integrate serial pupillary/corneal reflexes, motor responses, EEG background/seizures, bilateral N20 somatosensory evoked potentials, imaging and carefully interpreted biomarkers where locally available.
- No one test should be used in isolation to justify treatment withdrawal; allow additional time where confounders or inconclusive findings remain.
- ANZCOR’s 2024 post-resuscitation guideline explicitly endorses a multimodal approach [R05].

- For an examination scenario, describe the actual prognostication workflow rather than saying only “wait 72 hours”.
- First establish the chronology of ROSC, temperature management, seizure activity and sedative administration; review organ function and likely drug clearance, especially after long benzodiazepine or opioid infusions, hypothermia and AKI.
- Then perform serial examinations by experienced clinicians: pupillary light reflex (quantitative pupillometry where available), corneal reflexes and motor response.
- At 72 hours or later, absent pupillary/corneal reflexes may be concerning but are interpreted with other tests, not alone.
- Bilateral absence of the cortical N20 response on somatosensory evoked potentials, a highly malignant EEG background obtained without sedative confounding, markedly reduced grey/white matter differentiation on CT and diffuse restricted diffusion on appropriately timed MRI can each add information.
- Biomarker levels such as NSE depend on assay, timing, haemolysis and local validation; no universal serum cut-off should be applied without context [R05].

- Consider three broad diagnostic outcomes: a pattern supporting favourable prognosis, multiple concordant markers suggesting a poor prognosis, or an indeterminate result needing ongoing observation and repeat testing.
- Myoclonus early after arrest is not proof of hopeless prognosis: obtain EEG to distinguish epileptic from non-epileptic movements and assess the background.
- Prognostication guides discussions but does not replace a separate analysis of the patient's preferences, reversible illness and the burdens of continued therapy.
- This distinction reduces self-fulfilling withdrawal bias and is especially important when the original arrest was intraoperative and promptly witnessed.

## 5.7 Communication and follow-up after an arrest

- Communicate uncertainty appropriately: an early plan can explain what is known (cause treated, shock stabilised, oxygenation controlled), what is unknown (degree of neurological recovery), which tests are planned and when a reliable assessment may be possible.
- Avoid self-fulfilling pessimism from premature withdrawal.
- In survivors, assess cognition, mood, anxiety, depression, PTSD and physical function.
- Provide rehabilitation and follow-up rather than equating ICU discharge with complete recovery.
- These principles connect post-arrest care with the later chapter on post-intensive care syndrome.

items.title: 6. Why critically ill patients need both analgesia and a sedation strategy
items.body:
## 6.1 Pain, distress and wakefulness are different clinical problems

- Mechanically ventilated patients may experience surgical or injury pain, tube and line discomfort, dyspnoea, thirst, sleep disturbance, anxiety, delirium and fear.
- A patient who appears calm after propofol may still be in pain; a patient moving vigorously may be delirious or trying to signal an obstructed airway, under-ventilation, urinary retention or severe pain.
- **Analgesia-first, protocolised light sedation** therefore begins by asking what the patient’s distress represents, correcting a reversible problem and measuring pain separately from arousal.

- Uncontrolled pain drives sympathetic activity, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, increased oxygen consumption, ventilator dyssynchrony and distress, and may contribute to later traumatic memories.
- Conversely, excessive sedation is associated with prolonged ventilation, immobility, delirium, accumulation of medications, inability to participate in rehabilitation and masking of evolving neurological injury.
- Deep sedation is sometimes necessary—for severe ARDS with persistent dyssynchrony, raised ICP, refractory status epilepticus, procedural indications or neuromuscular blockade—but the justification and duration should be explicit.

## 6.2 Measure the desired effect before escalating drugs

| **Domain** | **Bedside tool** | **Interpretation and practical limitation** |
|---|---|---|
| Pain, communicative | 0–10 numerical rating scale | Ask patient directly; an observer’s estimate is not a substitute if the patient can respond |
| Pain, unable to report | Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT; 0–8) or Behavioural Pain Scale (BPS; 3–12) | CPOT considers facial expression, body movement, muscle tension and compliance/vocalisation; behaviour may be unreliable in deep paralysis or profound neurological dysfunction |
| Sedation/agitation | Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale (RASS, −5 to +4) | 0 alert/calm; −1 drowsy; −2 briefly awakens to voice; −3 movement/eye opening to voice without eye contact; −4 movement to physical stimulation; −5 unarousable; +1 restless to +4 combative |
| Delirium | CAM-ICU or ICDSC | CAM-ICU requires acute/fluctuating change and inattention with altered level of consciousness or disorganised thinking; not valid for unassessable deep sedation (e.g. RASS −4/−5) |
| Neuromuscular blockade | Peripheral nerve stimulator; objective TOF as indicated | Paralysed patient may experience pain and awareness without behavioural signs; ensure adequate analgesia and hypnosis independently |
| Sleep and circadian disturbance | Patient report, observational patterns, environmental review | Sedation does not equal restorative physiological sleep; noise, light, procedures and delirium worsen sleep quality |

- A reasonable default target for most ventilated adults is **RASS −1 to +1**, or a locally agreed light target such as 0 to −2 when clinical circumstances warrant.
- The exact target depends on analgesia, safety, breath-stacking, staffing, rescue plans and specific pathology.
- Document the goal on rounds and reassess at least each shift and after dose adjustments.
- If a patient becomes unexpectedly unresponsive, do not assume the infusion is simply too high: consider hypoxaemia, hypoglycaemia, seizures, stroke, intracranial bleeding, CO₂ narcosis and organ failure.

## 6.3 Analgesia: multimodal and mechanism-based

- Opioids remain central to acute pain treatment in ventilated patients, but choice matters.
- A nociceptive abdominal wound, fractured ribs, neuropathic pain, visceral distension and air hunger do not respond identically to one analgesic infusion.
- Provide regular simple analgesics when appropriate, regional techniques where safe, opioids titrated to effect, and targeted co-analgesics.
- Regional analgesia may reduce opioid requirement and improve respiratory mechanics in rib fractures or postoperative patients, but coagulopathy, infection, hypotension, peripheral neurological injury and anticoagulation must be considered.

- **Fentanyl** has rapid onset and haemodynamic stability at usual doses, but is lipophilic, may accumulate with prolonged infusion and has context-sensitive offset; consider reduced dosing in frail or shocked patients.
- **Remifentanil** has rapid predictable esterase metabolism and may facilitate a neurological examination, but requires continuous delivery; abrupt stopping can expose unmasked pain or withdrawal, and prolonged/high-dose use can promote acute opioid tolerance or hyperalgesia.
- **Morphine** produces active metabolites (notably morphine-6-glucuronide) that can accumulate in AKI and cause delayed sedation/respiratory depression. Histamine release can contribute to hypotension; use caution in unstable shock.
- **Hydromorphone** can be useful when morphine is poorly tolerated but its neuro-excitatory metabolite can accumulate in renal dysfunction. It is not automatically harmless in renal failure.
- **Ketamine** provides NMDA-antagonist analgesia, is opioid-sparing and may support blood pressure in some patients; catecholamine-depleted shock, myocardial ischaemia, hallucinations/dissociation and sympathetic stimulation require judgement.
  - Low-dose analgesic infusions are typically considerably lower than induction regimens (e.g. order-of-magnitude **0.05–0.3 mg/kg/h**, subject to local protocol).
- **Paracetamol** is an opioid-sparing adjunct if liver function and dosing permit; **NSAIDs** are often avoided in AKI, hypovolaemia, bleeding or high gastrointestinal risk.
- **Gabapentinoids** may help selected neuropathic pain but add sedation and require renal adjustment; routine use is not justified for all ventilated patients.

An analgesia plan also requires a route and reassessment: IV infusion in a ventilated unstable patient, enteral transition when absorptive function returns, and a planned taper when long-standing doses are used. Watch for oversedation, ileus, delirium, hypotension, hyperalgesia, tolerance and withdrawal rather than treating rising requirements solely by increasing opioid dose.

- Analgesia prescribing in ICU should account for type and location of pain, haemodynamics, organ dysfunction, ventilatory goals and the need to perform neurological examinations.
- Paracetamol can reduce opioid requirements for nociceptive pain (a common adult regimen is 1 g every 6 hours, maximum 4 g/day in suitable adults, with a lower maximum where low body mass, frailty or liver disease warrants).
- NSAIDs may be useful for selected inflammatory pain but are usually avoided during unstable AKI, active bleeding, platelet dysfunction, gastrointestinal ulceration or high-risk haemodynamic states.
- Regional techniques, including epidural or fascial-plane blocks, can be valuable after thoracic or abdominal injury, but anticoagulation, coagulopathy, infection and the ability to assess neurological complications must be addressed before performing them.

- For ongoing opioid therapy, fentanyl is readily titratable but accumulates in tissues after prolonged administration
- Morphine produces active renally cleared metabolites and can cause prolonged sedation or respiratory depression in renal impairment
- Hydromorphone also has a renally accumulating neuroexcitatory metabolite
- Remifentanil has rapid esterase clearance and permits neurological assessment but requires a plan for ongoing analgesia when stopped.
- Ketamine may reduce opioid burden and preserve sympathetic tone in selected patients, yet hallucinations, tachycardia or hypertension may be undesirable in others.
- Neuropathic pain may require a specific agent such as gabapentin or pregabalin, but these are sedating and renally eliminated, so start low with AKI/CRRT adjustments.
- Always reassess pain during turning, suctioning, coughing and mobilising rather than relying solely on a resting CPOT.

items.title: 7. Sedative pharmacology and selection in critical illness
items.priority: P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 7.1 Choosing a sedative is choosing its haemodynamic and recovery profile

- A hypnotic does not directly provide adequate analgesia, and no sedative reliably prevents delirium or post-intensive-care psychiatric sequelae by itself.
- Propofol and dexmedetomidine generally support titratable non-benzodiazepine sedation and facilitate awakening.
- Benzodiazepines remain valuable for specific indications including alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, convulsive seizures and some deeply sedated patients but are less attractive as default ICU sedatives because of accumulation and delirium associations.
- The **2025 SCCM PADIS update conditionally suggests dexmedetomidine rather than propofol where light sedation and/or reduction of delirium are top priorities**, based on new pooled trials, but this is not a universal superiority claim [R08].

| **Drug / typical adult infusion** | **Why useful** | **Important limits, physiology and adverse effects** |
|---|---|---|
| **Propofol** 0.3–3 mg/kg/h (higher occasionally with careful indication) | Rapid titration and wake-up; antiseizure/antiemetic actions; useful in high ICP | Dose-dependent vasodilatation, myocardial depression, respiratory depression; lipid calories and hypertriglyceridaemia; infection risks from emulsion handling; PRIS with high/prolonged doses |
| **Dexmedetomidine** ≈0.2–1.4 µg/kg/h, titrated (loading generally avoided in unstable ICU patients) | Cooperative/light sedation, analgesic sparing and minimal respiratory depression; useful near extubation | Bradycardia, hypotension; may not provide profound hypnosis for paralysis or severe dyssynchrony; withdrawal after prolonged infusion |
| **Midazolam** variable, commonly ≈0.02–0.1 mg/kg/h | Rapid anxiolysis, amnesia, anticonvulsant effect; usable for withdrawal/status | Context-sensitive accumulation; active metabolite accumulation in AKI; delirium, prolonged awakening, tolerance and withdrawal |
| **Clonidine** enteral or infusion under local protocol | α₂-agonism; weaning adjunct for sympathetic withdrawal | Bradycardia, hypotension, rebound hypertension if abruptly stopped |
| **Ketamine** subanaesthetic analgesic or sedative dosing as needed | Analgesia, bronchodilation, NMDA activity; opioid-sparing | Sympathetic changes, hallucinations, secretions; myocardial depression possible with catecholamine depletion |
| **Sevoflurane/isoflurane** via specialist ICU vaporising system | Rapid pulmonary elimination; alternative in selected refractory cases | Need scavenging and trained staff; environmental exposure, equipment logistics, pulmonary effects; not routine for every ICU |

These ranges illustrate relative order of magnitude rather than a prescribing protocol. Doses change substantially in the elderly, unstable, hypothermic, obese or organ-impaired patient; titrate to a documented clinical target and monitor respiratory and haemodynamic effects.

## 7.2 Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS)

- Propofol in high cumulative doses can impair mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and fatty-acid utilisation.
- PRIS is a potentially fatal syndrome characterised by otherwise unexplained **high-anion-gap/metabolic (often lactic) acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, arrhythmias/conduction abnormalities, cardiac failure, renal failure and hyperlipidaemia**, sometimes with hepatomegaly.
- Risk rises with prolonged high doses (historically **>4 mg/kg/h for >48 hours**, but it can occur outside this combination), severe critical illness, catecholamine or corticosteroid exposure, low carbohydrate supply and mitochondrial vulnerability.
- The 2020 and 2022 ANZCA examiner reports specifically examine recognition of PRIS; reciting the definition without prevention and management is insufficient.

- Prevent by using the lowest effective dose, avoiding unnecessarily prolonged high-dose propofol, monitoring triglycerides and acid–base/lactate, CK, potassium, renal function and ECG in prolonged/high-dose or deteriorating patients.
- At suspicion, **stop propofol immediately**, change to a suitable alternative, correct acidosis/hyperkalaemia/rhabdomyolysis and support circulation.
- Consider CRRT for renal indications and severe metabolic complications, and VA-ECMO in otherwise refractory cardiogenic collapse where available.
- Do not interpret new lactic acidosis in a septic patient on propofol as automatically sepsis progression without assessing PRIS.

## 7.3 Dexmedetomidine versus propofol: what the trials actually show

- Propofol infusion syndrome deserves a differential and surveillance plan, not only a named complication.
- It is associated with high/prolonged propofol exposure (classically >4 mg/kg/h for >48 hours), severe critical illness, catecholamine or steroid therapy and impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid utilisation, although cases can occur outside those thresholds.
- The dangerous syndrome combines otherwise unexplained high-anion-gap/lactic acidosis, myocardial dysfunction or arrhythmias, raised creatine kinase/rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, renal injury and often hypertriglyceridaemia.
- It may be confused with worsening sepsis, shock, ischaemia or seizures.
- If suspected, stop propofol immediately, change to an alternative sedative, investigate potassium, ABG/lactate, CK, triglycerides, ECG/echo, renal/liver function and institute circulatory and metabolic rescue; RRT or ECPR may be needed in refractory cases.
- Screening tests do not make ongoing high-dose propofol safe in a deteriorating patient.

- Severe hypertriglyceridaemia and pancreatitis can also occur without full PRIS.
- A lipid formulation given at 1.1 kcal/mL contributes to total energy—propofol 15 mL/h provides approximately 396 kcal/day before any enteral nutrition, IV dextrose or citrate-containing solutions.
- This is relevant both to overfeeding during prolonged sedation and to dangerous unrecognised calorie exposure in patients at high refeeding risk.
- Do not assume sedative calories deliver useful protein, electrolytes or micronutrients.

- The Australasian **SPICE III** trial randomised approximately 4,000 mechanically ventilated adults to early dexmedetomidine or usual sedative care and found **no difference in 90-day mortality (29.1% versus 29.1%)**; bradycardia/hypotension were more frequent in the dexmedetomidine group, and many patients needed supplemental sedatives [R09].
- **MENDS2**, a trial of 422 ventilated adults with sepsis, found no significant advantage of dexmedetomidine over propofol in days alive without delirium/coma at 14 days, ventilator-free days or 90-day mortality [R10].
- **NONSEDA** did not show a 90-day mortality benefit from a strategy of no sedation versus light sedation with daily interruption [R11].

- These individual RCT findings do not contradict the 2025 PADIS focused update: pooled evidence across more trials conditionally favoured dexmedetomidine for some delirium-related outcomes, especially where light sedation is the goal [R08].
- The right inference is **patient-centred selection with a target of wakefulness**, not routine high-dose dexmedetomidine for all patients or a promise of survival benefit.

## 7.4 Critical illness changes pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics

- Traditional induction pharmacokinetics cannot simply be transposed onto several weeks of ICU infusions.
- **Distribution** changes with capillary leak, oedema, ascites, hypoalbuminaemia, obesity, increased extracellular fluid and fluid resuscitation.
- Water-soluble drugs may have a larger apparent volume of distribution; highly protein-bound drugs may have greater unbound fraction, although total measured concentration can mislead.
- **Clearance** changes with hepatic hypoperfusion, cholestasis, liver failure, AKI, augmented renal clearance, inflammation-mediated downregulation of enzymes, hypothermia and extracorporeal devices.
- Continuous infusions lead to accumulation in peripheral compartments and a progressively prolonged context-sensitive offset; lipophilic agents such as fentanyl and midazolam are affected substantially.

**Pharmacodynamic sensitivity also changes:**

- Older age, delirium, acute brain injury, electrolyte imbalance, shock and concomitant opioids may increase effects at a given concentration.
- In severe shock, even ketamine can depress myocardial contractility when adrenergic reserves are exhausted.
- ECMO circuits can adsorb lipophilic drugs (especially early), while CRRT removes some hydrophilic low-protein-bound compounds variably according to membrane and effluent dose; avoid crude assumptions that “renal failure increases every sedative” or that CRRT normalises all clearance.
- In a daily review, ask whether the patient’s observed dose requirement reflects tolerance, pain/delirium, evolving organ function, circuit changes or an undiagnosed problem.

- Critical illness changes both concentration and effect.
- Early capillary leak, positive fluid balance and hypoalbuminaemia increase the apparent volume of distribution of some drugs and can increase the free fraction of highly protein-bound agents.
- Later organ failure reduces metabolism or excretion; a serum creatinine that is apparently stable may conceal a changing clearance because creatinine generation is reduced by muscle loss.
- Liver dysfunction decreases clearance of many benzodiazepines and opioids, while AKI causes accumulation of active morphine and midazolam metabolites.
- Temperature, acid–base changes and altered blood–brain barrier permeability can change responsiveness even when plasma concentration is unchanged.

- Extracorporeal circuits introduce further uncertainty: ECMO tubing and oxygenators may sequester lipophilic/protein-bound sedatives and analgesics, especially early after circuit change, while a larger extracorporeal volume affects some drug concentrations.
- CRRT clearance depends on molecular size, free fraction, effluent dose, membrane characteristics and whether drug metabolism remains adequate; high CRRT flow does not reliably prevent accumulation of active metabolites.
- Practical management is to titrate to the observed pain and sedation target, check trends in organ support, note circuit changes, and plan a daily wake-up assessment when safe.
- This is why an infusion rate used uneventfully in a normal patient cannot simply be copied to a patient with evolving hepatic failure or ECMO support.

items.title: 8. The practical ICU sedation and analgesia pathway: assessment, interruption, liberation and withdrawal
items.body:
## 8.1 A daily clinical sequence rather than automatic infusion continuation

- Begin with the patient’s immediate goals.
- Review underlying pain sources, ventilation, haemodynamic stability, neurological state, sleep, mobilisation, medication accumulation, family interaction and procedure plans.
- Correct dyspnoea, obstruction, ventilator dyssynchrony, constipation, retention, unmet thirst and delirium triggers before increasing hypnosis.
- Assess CPOT/NRS and RASS; set goals and choose the least burdensome intervention.

This is the rationale of the **ABCDEF** bundle:

- Assess/manage pain.
- Spontaneous awakening and breathing trial coordination.
- Choice of sedation.
- Delirium identification, prevention and treatment.
- Early mobility.
- Family engagement.

- An awakening trial (spontaneous awakening trial, SAT) means temporarily stopping or reducing a continuous hypnotic when safe, with the aim of assessing consciousness and whether ongoing sedation is required.
- Screen for contraindications first: refractory seizures, uncontrolled intracranial pressure, severe agitation with an unsafe airway, active neuromuscular blockade, severe ARDS requiring deep sedation for synchrony, ongoing resuscitation or urgent procedure.
- Monitor heart rate, BP, SpO₂, respiratory status, distress and line safety; resume at a lower, appropriate dose if the trial fails.
- Coordinate with a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT), but do not confuse a successful SAT with readiness to extubate.
- Extubation also requires adequate airway protection, manageable secretions, cough, gas exchange and a plan for post-extubation respiratory support.

- Daily interruption is not mandatory when sedation is already reliably minimal and a wakeful target is achieved; the objective is **a consistently reviewed low-sedation state**, not ritualised stopping regardless of context.
- Multiple days of deep sedation increase risks of weakness, delirium and drug accumulation.
- Non-pharmacological care—daylight, quiet nights, hearing/vision aids, familiar voices, orientation, glasses, early mobilisation, sleep consolidation and communication aids—supports the strategy.
- The 2025 PADIS update conditionally supports enhanced mobilisation/rehabilitation and melatonin in suitable adults, while finding insufficient evidence for routine antipsychotics specifically to treat delirium [R08].

## 8.2 Delirium is an acute organ-dysfunction syndrome, not merely agitation

- Delirium is an acute/fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness and cognition caused by underlying disease, medications and environmental factors.
- It may be **hyperactive**, **hypoactive** (easily missed) or mixed.
- Consider sepsis, hypoxaemia, metabolic/electrolyte abnormalities, renal/hepatic encephalopathy, CNS pathology, pain, anticholinergic exposure, benzodiazepines, sleep loss and withdrawal.
- CAM-ICU or ICDSC screening works only in patients arousable enough to be assessed; reassess after reducing sedation when feasible.
- A patient pulling at lines may be delirious, in pain, confused by unfamiliar surroundings or struggling with ventilation.
- Physical restraints can be necessary for immediate safety but can worsen distress and should not substitute for identifying the cause.

- Prevention includes light sedation, minimising benzodiazepines where possible, early mobility, consistent circadian cues, sleep protection, hearing/vision aids, family engagement and analgesia.
- Treat dangerous agitation with the smallest appropriate rescue therapy when the patient presents immediate harm; antipsychotics may be used short term for severe distress or safety indications, but have not consistently improved important delirium outcomes in trials.
- Consider QTc prolongation, torsades risk, Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia and extrapyramidal effects.
- Dexmedetomidine may be useful when agitation precludes weaning/extubation but does not remove the need to treat delirium causes.

## 8.3 Tolerance, iatrogenic withdrawal and the physiology of gradual weaning

- After several days of continuous opioids, benzodiazepines or α₂-agonists, receptor adaptation and neuroendocrine counter-regulation create physiological dependence.
- Abrupt dose reductions can produce sympathetic activation, agitation, pain, tremor, diarrhoea, sweating, hypertension, tachycardia, fever, insomnia and occasionally seizures (especially benzodiazepine withdrawal).
- This syndrome overlaps with sepsis, delirium and inadequate analgesia; distinguishing them requires a medication timeline and systematic assessment.
- Opioid withdrawal is often characterised by autonomic/GI symptoms and pain; benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause seizures and serious delirium; dexmedetomidine or clonidine withdrawal may produce rebound sympathetic hypertension/tachycardia.

- For patients receiving only short low-dose sedation, simple cessation with monitoring may be sufficient.
- For patients receiving prolonged high-dose therapy, a **structured, individualised taper** is safer.
- A common approach is to calculate recent 24-hour total exposure, identify a stable enteral alternative where useful, reduce the infusion in small increments (often **10–20% per day** as tolerated, slower for prolonged/high-dose exposure or previous withdrawal), and monitor objective signs.
- Transition from IV fentanyl or remifentanil to scheduled enteral opioid may help, taking equianalgesic uncertainty and incomplete cross-tolerance into account; do not treat conversion charts as exact.
- Some teams use clonidine to attenuate α₂-agonist or opioid-associated sympathetic symptoms, watching for hypotension.
- In refractory benzodiazepine withdrawal, a longer-acting agent such as diazepam or enteral lorazepam may be used if hepatic and renal function permit.
- Avoid loading the patient with a second long-lived drug without a clear rationale.

- An explicit withdrawal-management plan should distinguish physiologic dependence from addiction.
- In adult ICU patients there is no single validated withdrawal scale or universally proven taper protocol; published studies use inconsistent definitions and interventions.
- A 2025 scoping review found reported iatrogenic-withdrawal incidence spanning roughly 14–50%, but this wide range reflects differences in populations and diagnostic criteria, and evidence for preventative pharmacological substitution is limited [R33].
- The frequently used 10–20% daily reduction is therefore an illustrative bedside starting approach, not a guideline-mandated schedule and not appropriate for every drug or duration.

- Before each change, document the cumulative daily opioid/benzodiazepine exposure, prior baseline medication use, concurrent clonidine/dexmedetomidine and relevant hepatic/renal dysfunction.
- A patient developing unexplained sweating, yawning, diarrhoea, mydriasis, tachycardia and worsening pain as fentanyl is reduced may have opioid withdrawal; tremor, perceptual disturbance, hypertension and seizures after midazolam withdrawal raise concern for benzodiazepine withdrawal.
- Simultaneously exclude sepsis, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, delirium and inadequate analgesia.
- Some patients need a planned longer-acting enteral substitute, but conversion factors are imprecise after prolonged infusions, organ failure and incomplete cross-tolerance; consult a local pharmacist and titrate to response.
- Pause or slow the taper when clinically significant withdrawal appears, treat distress, protect against respiratory suppression and clearly hand over the plan to the ward.

**Weaning and delirium treatment are linked:**

- A distressed ventilated patient with tachycardia may need analgesia, an opioid taper, treatment of infection, sleep, family reassurance or a more gradual change—not an immediate escalation of propofol.
- Document a written plan, symptoms to monitor, maximum acceptable adjustment rate, rescue doses, and which team will continue the taper on the ward.
- A patient transferred from ICU with no documentation of prior opioid/benzodiazepine exposure may develop unrecognised withdrawal in the next 24–72 hours.

## 8.4 Example: planning liberation after a 14-day ventilation course

- An adult with severe pneumonia received fentanyl 100–200 µg/h and midazolam 2–6 mg/h over 14 days, and now has improving oxygenation and haemodynamics.
- Begin with objective pain/delirium assessment and check hepatic/renal function; new tachycardia is not automatically a sign of persistent infection.
- Reduce midazolam and move to a lighter, titratable sedation plan, with repeated wakefulness assessments and SBTs.
- Identify the current pain requirement before stopping fentanyl; consider a scheduled enteral agent with carefully reduced equivalent dosing if dependence is likely.
- Track withdrawal symptoms and implement preventive nonpharmacological care.
- Set a timeline tied to clinical response rather than a rigid number of days, reassessing both ventilator readiness and medication burden daily.

items.title: 9. The stress response, catabolism and metabolic phases of critical illness
items.body:
## 9.1 From the initial insult to prolonged organ dysfunction

- Major trauma, infection, surgery and shock activate afferent neural signalling, sympathetic output, the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, proinflammatory cytokines and the innate immune response.
- Catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and growth hormone support urgent energy availability but simultaneously increase gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, insulin resistance and protein breakdown.
- The liver synthesises acute-phase proteins while skeletal muscle releases amino acids (particularly alanine and glutamine) to fuel gluconeogenesis, immune cells and repair.
- When prolonged, this response reduces respiratory-muscle and limb-muscle strength, prolongs ventilator dependence and impairs rehabilitation.

- Classical descriptions distinguish an **ebb phase** (hours after severe injury: hypoperfusion, limited oxygen delivery, often lower metabolic rate) from a subsequent **flow phase** (catabolic, hyperdynamic/hypermetabolic response).
- These are useful conceptual frameworks rather than discrete clinical switches: sepsis, sedation, nutrition, fever and organ support modify the pattern, and many ICU patients have overlapping inflammation, immunosuppression and persistent catabolism.
- The early response prioritises survival over growth; feeding a critically shocked patient to a calculated “full target” cannot automatically reverse hormonally driven muscle proteolysis.

## 9.2 Metabolic consequences at the bedside

- **Hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance:** catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and cytokines increase endogenous glucose production despite exogenous carbohydrate.
  - Stress hyperglycaemia should be treated without triggering hypoglycaemia; a common ICU range is approximately **6–10 mmol/L** (often acceptable up to 10 according to protocol and context), using an infusion when needed and frequent monitoring.
- **Proteolysis and negative nitrogen balance:** muscle loss occurs even if energy targets appear achieved. Early mobilisation, adequate-but-not-excessive protein as tolerated and correction of organ dysfunction contribute to recovery, but high early protein dosing has not reliably improved hard outcomes in trials.
- **Changes in fat metabolism:** increased lipolysis provides fatty acids, but mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired lipoprotein clearance can worsen hypertriglyceridaemia, especially with propofol or lipid-based parenteral nutrition.
- **Water and electrolyte redistribution:** ADH and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone activation favour sodium/water retention; inflammation and capillary leak expand extracellular fluid, while intracellular depletion and electrolyte shifts may coexist with oedema.
  - Refeeding and insulin shift phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly.
- **Immune and gut changes:** intestinal dysmotility, splanchnic hypoperfusion, antibiotics, microbiome disruption, mucosal injury and hyperglycaemia affect tolerance and infection risk.

- The metabolic stress response helps explain why malnutrition and overfeeding can coexist.
- In the acute phase, endogenous glucose production and glycogenolysis continue despite nutrient infusion, so forcing a full glucose-calorie target may produce substantial hyperglycaemia and lipogenesis without suppressing catabolism.
- Skeletal muscle becomes a fuel reservoir for acute-phase protein synthesis and gluconeogenesis.
- Negative nitrogen balance is useful conceptually: approximately 6.25 g of protein corresponds to 1 g of nitrogen; estimated nitrogen loss may be inferred from urinary urea nitrogen plus other losses, though AKI and RRT reduce measurement reliability.
- Nitrogen balance should not drive aggressive high protein administration in early severe multiorgan failure without considering the EFFORT Protein evidence.

- Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression and catabolism after a long ICU course (often termed PICS in critical-care physiology literature—distinct from the abbreviation for post-intensive care syndrome) can cause recurrent infections, lymphopenia, progressive lean-mass loss and poor rehabilitation.
- During the recovery phase the nutritional priority increasingly shifts toward adequate protein, energy and resistance/mobility rehabilitation, but the timing is guided by haemodynamic stability, organ dysfunction and demonstrated tolerance, not a fixed ICU-day number.

## 9.3 When the inflammatory response does not resolve

- Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression and catabolism can produce a prolonged ICU phenotype involving recurrent infections, poor wound healing, sarcopenia, endocrine dysregulation and functional dependence.
- In ICU-acquired weakness, critical illness polyneuropathy and myopathy may coexist, particularly after sepsis, multiorgan failure, hyperglycaemia, immobility and certain drug exposures.
- Prevention is multifactorial: early haemodynamic stabilisation, appropriate infection control and nutrition, minimising deep sedation/immobility, glucose avoidance at extremes and rehabilitation.
- A single immunonutrient, hormone or “high-protein” formula has not been shown to reverse the entire syndrome.

items.title: 10. Prescribing nutrition: assessment, energy expenditure, protein and timing
items.body:
## 10.1 Why nutrition prescribing is not simply using a calorie calculator

- A useful nutrition prescription states **indication, risk of malnutrition/refeeding, route, energy target, protein target, timing of advancement, fluid/electrolytes, monitoring and a contingency plan**.
- An overweight patient may still have sarcopenia; a low albumin during critical illness reflects inflammation and capillary leak as much as nutrition and is not a reliable stand-alone marker of malnutrition.
- Review preadmission weight trend, intake, clinical muscle/fat loss, functional status, gastrointestinal tract, swallowing, chronic illness and risk of refeeding.

- Indirect calorimetry, measuring oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production, is preferred when feasible for energy expenditure, but its accuracy depends on stable gas exchange and equipment; high FiO₂, air leaks and extracorporeal support can invalidate measurements.
- When calorimetry is unavailable, a pragmatic early estimate of **20–25 kcal/kg/day** (patient-specific adjusted/ideal body weight if appropriate) is commonly used rather than a mathematically precise target.
- Critically ill energy expenditure is variable and changes across phases.
- Predictive formulae (e.g. Harris–Benedict) can be substantially inaccurate.
- Energy from **propofol (1.1 kcal/mL), dextrose infusions and citrate solutions** counts towards total caloric delivery; ignoring it can cause unintended overfeeding.

- The 2023 ESPEN practical ICU guideline generally favours **progressive feeding**, especially avoiding early delivery beyond measured or estimated energy expenditure, rather than immediate full feeding [R12].
- If indirect calorimetry is used, energy provision is progressively increased according to phase and tolerance.
- The exact target and speed depend on nutritional risk, ongoing shock, ability to absorb and organ function.
- **Do not prescribe 25–30 kcal/kg plus large propofol calories by default on ICU day 1.**

## 10.2 Protein is not interchangeable with calories

- Protein supports immune function, wound healing and maintenance of lean mass; caloric adequacy does not ensure protein sufficiency.
- Conversely, early aggressive protein loading in severe critical illness cannot reliably overcome catabolism and may be harmful in some settings.
- Many ICU recommendations target a gradual approach towards approximately **1.2–1.3 g/kg/day** as the acute phase resolves, individualised for obesity, wounds, RRT, hepatic failure and renal function.
- **EFFORT Protein** randomised high nutritional-risk ventilated adults to prescribed ≥2.2 versus ≤1.2 g/kg/day and found no improvement in discharge alive; a signal of possible harm was seen in AKI and high organ-failure subgroups [R13].
- This evidence argues against a reflexive “more protein is always better” approach.

- In an obese patient, calculate requirements using an appropriate reference weight and a dietitian-supported protocol rather than blindly applying actual body weight.
- In AKI without RRT, avoid both marked protein deficiency and high-dose loading; in CRRT, amino acid loss may require a higher individualized provision during recovery.
- The phase of illness is at least as important as the diagnosis.

- A worked nutritional prescription should begin with four values: likely energy expenditure, safe early fraction of that expenditure, protein goal and non-feed calories.
- Suppose an 80 kg adult is mechanically ventilated following septic shock, is now haemodynamically stabilising, and measured indirect calorimetry is unavailable.
- A rough predictive estimate might be 20–25 kcal/kg/day (1600–2000 kcal/day) but is less reliable than measured energy expenditure, especially with obesity, fever or sedation.
- Early in critical illness, a progressive hypocaloric strategy—not immediate 100% delivery—is appropriate.
- For example, a clinician might begin trophic EN at 20 mL/h of a 1 kcal/mL formula (480 kcal/day) once perfusion is acceptable and advance in response to haemodynamics, glucose, bowel function and electrolytes.
- If propofol is running at 15 mL/h, its approximately 396 kcal/day must be included in the day's energy accounting; this does not provide the protein the patient needs.

- Protein prescription is a separate calculation, not the residual caloric requirement.
- A pragmatic eventual target may be around 1.2–1.3 g/kg/day where suitable, approximately 96–104 g/day for this patient, advanced with clinical recovery and adjusted for kidney status and nutrition risk.
- Standard 1 kcal/mL enteral feeds may contain only 40–60 g of protein per litre, so delivering target energy does not automatically deliver target protein.
- Options include a higher-protein formula or measured modular supplement.
- Avoid reflexively giving ≥2.2 g/kg/day early in severe illness: the EFFORT Protein trial found no improvement in recovery and a possible adverse signal in AKI and high organ-failure subgroups [R13, R34].

- In obesity, actual body weight overestimates metabolically active tissue and a simple 25 kcal/kg actual weight formula may overfeed.
- Prefer indirect calorimetry; if unavailable, adjusted/ideal body weight is often used per local nutrition guidelines.
- For a patient with high-output CRRT, protein losses into effluent and ongoing catabolism may increase later requirements, while severe AKI not on KRT raises concern about high early protein loading.
- A burn patient, major trauma patient and chronically malnourished patient therefore cannot safely be prescribed an identical caloric and protein plan solely by multiplying scale weight.

## 10.3 Enteral is preferred when the gastrointestinal tract can be used safely

- Early enteral nutrition (EN), generally started **within 24–48 hours after stabilisation**, maintains gastrointestinal use, is usually simpler than PN and avoids central line/compounding-associated risks.
- However, **uncontrolled shock with escalating vasopressors and intestinal hypoperfusion is not the moment for full-dose gastric feeding**.
- Reassess after resuscitation: stable/decreasing pressor requirements, acceptable lactate trend and no signs of bowel ischaemia may allow cautious trophic EN.
- A low-to-moderate vasopressor dose alone is not an absolute contraindication; the trajectory and perfusion context matter.

- Absolute or strong contraindications to initiating EN include **uncontrolled shock, bowel ischaemia, intestinal obstruction, uncontrolled gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal compartment syndrome with impaired perfusion and situations in which gastrointestinal continuity is absent or unsafe**.
- Other barriers are relative: gastric residuals, high gastric output, ileus, severe vomiting, high aspiration risk and acute pancreatitis in which tolerable post-pyloric feeding may be preferred.
- A mechanically ventilated patient is not automatically unable to receive gastric feeding.
- Raise head of bed ≈30–45°, ensure tube position according to protocol, avoid unnecessary sedation, use a bowel regimen, and consider prokinetics or post-pyloric feeding for persistent gastric intolerance.

**Example prescription for a 70-kg adult:**

- Begin a standard enteral formula at a conservative rate (e.g. **20–30 mL/h**) after shock stabilises; review glucose, electrolytes, gastric symptoms and pressor trajectory.
