- If using 1 kcal/mL, 30 mL/h provides 720 kcal/day before interruptions, protein and non-feed calories.
- Gradually increase to a measured or estimated requirement over several days while separately checking grams of protein supplied.
- If a patient on propofol 20 mL/h receives 528 kcal/day from the sedative emulsion, count this in energy planning but not in protein.
- The feed is a provisional prescription, not a commitment to reach full targets irrespective of intolerance.

- The safety decision about enteral nutrition is primarily about perfusion and intestinal viability, not merely whether a patient is on any vasopressor.
- Avoid or delay EN in uncontrolled shock with rising lactate/escalating vasopressors, suspected bowel ischaemia or obstruction, abdominal compartment syndrome, uncontrolled upper GI bleeding or other clear contraindications.
- Once the circulation is resuscitated and pressor needs are stable or declining, low-dose gastric EN can often be introduced with monitoring.
- In NUTRIREA-3, early low-calorie/low-protein feeding in ventilated adults with shock did not reduce 90-day mortality compared with standard targets but reduced vomiting, diarrhoea and bowel ischaemia—an important reason not to aggressively push full feed in a patient still requiring major vasoactive support [R16].

- Feed intolerance requires diagnosis, not automatically abandoning the gut.
- Examine the abdomen and review escalating pressors, opioid dose, electrolyte abnormalities, ileus, distension, diarrhoea, vomiting and medication-related problems.
- Correct the cause, consider a prokinetic such as IV metoclopramide where appropriate (commonly 10 mg up to every 8 hours, with renal-dose reduction and awareness of QT/extrapyramidal adverse effects) or erythromycin for short-term use, and consider post-pyloric access for recurrent gastric intolerance or significant aspiration risk.
- Gastric residual volume alone is a poor measure of aspiration risk; use an institutional threshold and the whole clinical picture.
- Abdominal pain, bloody aspirate/stool, rapidly rising lactate and increasing pressor requirement during feeding should trigger urgent assessment for intestinal ischaemia and feed cessation.

## 10.4 When to use parenteral nutrition (PN)

- PN is appropriate when the gut cannot be safely used or the expected EN deficit is prolonged and clinically important, especially in patients with severe pre-existing malnutrition.
- It requires safe central or suitable peripheral access, sterile compounding, an individualised provision of amino acids, dextrose, lipid, electrolytes, trace elements and vitamins, and close biochemical monitoring.
- **Early supplemental PN is not universally beneficial**.
- The **EPaNIC** trial found that deferring supplemental PN until day 8 in a population receiving an early enteral protocol resulted in fewer infections and faster recovery without a mortality penalty compared with early supplemental PN [R14].
- This does not mean a severely malnourished patient with an unusable gut should always be left without nutrition for a week.
- Consider risks, baseline reserve, expected gut recovery and an individualised plan.

- PN complications include **catheter infection, thrombosis, hyperglycaemia, fluid overload, electrolyte disturbances/refeeding, hepatic steatosis/cholestasis, hypertriglyceridaemia and micronutrient imbalance**.
- EN complications include aspiration, regurgitation, diarrhoea, abdominal distension, overfeeding and, rarely but importantly, mesenteric ischaemia in poorly perfused patients.
- Both routes can cause refeeding syndrome.
- Compare routes by indication and physiological risk, not by the assumption that one is always harmless.

- Parenteral nutrition is a complex prescription requiring control of energy, protein (amino acids), carbohydrate, lipid, water, electrolytes, minerals, vitamins and trace elements.
- It is indicated when the gut cannot safely or adequately be used for a sufficiently prolonged period, rather than because a patient misses a single day's target calories.
- In the first ICU week, routine full-dose PN can worsen overfeeding and metabolic complications: EPaNIC found that delaying supplemental PN in many patients reduced some complications and accelerated recovery compared with early supplementation [R14].
- But the genuinely malnourished patient, prolonged intestinal failure, bowel ischaemia, high-output fistula or short-bowel syndrome may warrant a different, earlier specialist strategy.

- A safe daily PN review checks central-access need and line infection risk
- Prescribed glucose infusion and actual glucose values
- Triglycerides and propofol lipid exposure
- K, Mg, phosphate and calcium
- Renal function and acid–base
- Sodium/water balance
- Liver tests and cholestasis
- Drug/solution compatibility
- And whether enteral feeding can now replace some PN.
- Sudden cessation of a high-dextrose PN infusion can create glycaemic issues if insulin continues.
- Trace-element requirements change with renal replacement and severe hepatic cholestasis, so discuss such prescriptions with ICU dietetics and pharmacy.

## 10.5 Evidence that changes how nutrition is advanced

- The **TARGET** trial (nearly 4,000 mechanically ventilated adults in Australasian ICUs) compared energy-dense 1.5 kcal/mL with routine 1.0 kcal/mL feeding at similar volumes and found **no improvement in 90-day survival** with approximately 600 kcal/day more energy [R15].
- **NUTRIREA-3**, in vasopressor-dependent ventilated patients, compared low early calories/protein (6 kcal/kg/day; 0.2–0.4 g/kg/day protein) with standard (25 kcal/kg/day; 1.0–1.3 g/kg/day) and found **no significant 90-day mortality difference**; the lower-intake group had shorter time to ICU discharge readiness and fewer gastrointestinal complications including bowel ischaemia [R16].
- **EFFORT Protein** found no benefit from early very high protein dosing, with caution in AKI [R13].
- Collectively these trials challenge rapid full-target feeding in severe early critical illness; they do **not** support indefinite starvation or protein deficiency during rehabilitation.

items.title: 11. Refeeding syndrome and other nutrition complications
items.body:
## 11.1 Mechanism: insulin unmasks intracellular depletion

- Starvation reduces insulin, promotes fat oxidation and depletes whole-body phosphate, potassium, magnesium and thiamine, even when the serum concentration of some electrolytes remains near normal.
- Abrupt carbohydrate delivery produces insulin release and drives electrolytes into cells.
- Phosphate depletion reduces ATP and 2,3-DPG and may cause weakness, respiratory failure, haemolysis and cardiac dysfunction; hypokalaemia/magnesaemia cause arrhythmias, while thiamine deficiency impairs carbohydrate oxidation and can precipitate lactic acidosis, cardiac failure and Wernicke encephalopathy.
- Sodium/fluid retention compounds the risk.
- Consequently, **the patient’s nutritional history can be more predictive of risk than a single pre-feeding phosphate value**.

- Risk factors include prolonged inadequate intake (particularly >5–10 days), major recent weight loss, very low BMI, alcohol dependence, eating disorders, chronic malabsorption, refeeding after prolonged ICU catabolism, low initial phosphate/potassium/magnesium and certain drug exposures.
- ASPEN criteria define refeeding syndrome by a fall in one or more of phosphate, potassium or magnesium of **10–20% (mild), 20–30% (moderate), or >30% and/or associated organ dysfunction (severe)** within five days of reintroduction/substantial increase of energy [R17].

## 11.2 Prevent, recognise and treat

- Before nutrition, assess risk and measure phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose; give **thiamine before initiating significant carbohydrate** in high-risk patients (commonly **100–200 mg IV/enteral daily**, with more intensive regimens when Wernicke’s encephalopathy is suspected).
- Start nutrition conservatively in high-risk patients and advance according to electrolyte stability and clinical response.
- Monitor phosphate, magnesium and potassium frequently (e.g. **12-hourly for 72 hours** in marked risk, more frequently if unstable), fluid balance, ECG and signs of weakness.
- Replace depleted electrolytes promptly by an appropriate route according to severity and renal function; monitor for recurrent shifts.

- If significant **refeeding hypophosphataemia** develops, ESPEN advises restricting energy delivery for approximately **48 hours** with gradual re-advancement, while correcting electrolytes and maintaining vital micronutrients [R12].
- Do not abruptly discontinue every nutrient without treating thiamine deficiency or reassessing the patient’s current state.
- Severe symptomatic hypophosphataemia requires IV phosphate according to local replacement protocols; phosphate formulations contain sodium or potassium and should be selected according to potassium, renal function and calcium–phosphate risks.

- For an examination candidate, risk classification and diagnosis are separate.
- The NICE high-risk criteria include any single major risk factor (BMI <16 kg/m², >15% unintentional weight loss over 3–6 months, little/no intake >10 days or low K/phosphate/Mg before feeding), or two less severe factors (BMI <18.5, >10% weight loss, intake absent >5 days, or a history of alcohol misuse/insulin/chemotherapy/antacid/diuretic exposure).
- An extreme-risk example is BMI <14 or negligible intake >15 days.
- A patient can have normal serum phosphate before feeding despite profound whole-body depletion [R35].

- A NICE-style plan in a high-risk adult begins at no more than approximately 10 kcal/kg/day, or 5 kcal/kg/day in extreme-risk patients with close cardiac monitoring, advancing cautiously toward full needs over four to seven days according to clinical and biochemical response.
- Thiamine 200–300 mg daily is given immediately before and during early feeding (often about ten days in the NICE regimen), alongside other vitamins and monitored K, Mg and phosphate replacement.
- ASPEN suggests 100–200 mg thiamine before refeeding and uses a slightly different advancement strategy; follow the local high-risk pathway and do not mix its numbers indiscriminately with NICE.
- Count every source of energy: enteral feeds, PN, IV dextrose and the propofol lipid load.
- Clinically unstable electrolyte deficiency may require temporarily pausing advancement while replacement proceeds; severe arrhythmia or cardiac failure requires emergency treatment [R17, R35].

- ASPEN's diagnostic criteria classify mild, moderate and severe refeeding syndrome by a fall in serum phosphate, potassium or magnesium within five days of calorie introduction: 10–20%, 20–30% and >30% respectively, or organ dysfunction attributable to these changes/thiamine deficiency for severe disease.
- The pathophysiology connects insulin secretion with intracellular phosphate consumption, potassium/magnesium shifts, sodium-water retention and increased myocardial work.
- Consequences include ventricular arrhythmia, acute heart failure, respiratory-muscle weakness and failure to wean, seizures, Wernicke encephalopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
- Monitoring in high-risk ICU patients usually requires baseline electrolytes and at least daily testing, often 12-hourly during unstable initiation, plus fluid balance, glucose and cardiac observation.
- These measures are treatment, not simply a lab checklist [R17].

## 11.3 Other high-yield complications and how they appear clinically

| **Complication** | **Mechanism and recognition** | **Prevention / management** |
|---|---|---|
| Aspiration associated with EN | Regurgitation, impaired protective reflexes, gastric dysmotility; new hypoxaemia/infiltrates | Elevate head, appropriate tube verification, assess sedation and gastric intolerance, prokinetics/post-pyloric route when indicated |
| Feed intolerance | Vomiting, abdominal distension, large residuals, diarrhoea or high gastric output; may signify hypoperfusion | Reassess perfusion and bowel examination, medications and formula; consider reducing rate, prokinetic, post-pyloric access |
| Mesenteric ischaemia | Severe abdominal distension/pain (if awake), rising lactate, bloody stools, escalating shock; very high mortality | Stop EN and urgently evaluate when suspected; correct perfusion and obtain surgical review; do not dismiss as simple ileus |
| Hyperglycaemia | Stress insulin resistance plus dextrose; infection and osmotic consequences | Glucose monitoring, appropriate insulin protocol, avoid excessive carbohydrate |
| Overfeeding | Excess CO₂ production, hyperglycaemia, fatty liver, hypertriglyceridaemia, difficult ventilator weaning | Count propofol/dextrose calories and avoid rapid full-target provision |
| PN catheter infection / thrombosis | Fever, bloodstream infection, limb/neck swelling, catheter malfunction | Aseptic access and line review, discontinue unnecessary access, culture and treat/remove when indicated |
| Micronutrient deficits | Prolonged restricted intake or nutrient losses; thiamine deficiency, trace deficiencies | Standard supplementation, individualised monitoring for long stays/RRT/high losses |

The nutrition prescription should be revised after major physiological change: a new vasopressor escalation, bowel surgery, renal replacement initiation, improved swallowing or prolonged rehabilitation all change the optimal route and dose.

items.title: 12. Illness-severity scores: what they measure, how to interpret them and why they can mislead
items.body:
## 12.1 The clinical question dictates which score is appropriate

- A severity score can standardise descriptions of physiological disturbance, compare cohorts, monitor change, facilitate research or audit, and estimate risk in populations.
- It cannot replace diagnosis, identify an individual patient’s optimal treatment or certify futility.
- If a patient has a SOFA score of 12, the essential clinical questions are which organs are failing, is dysfunction worsening, why is that happening, and which failure is reversible?
- A numerical score without this interpretation does not provide a management plan.

- **Admission prognostic scores** such as APACHE II/III/IV and SAPS use physiology, age and other factors to estimate population risk.
- **Serial organ-dysfunction scores** such as SOFA are suited to describing organ failure and trends.
- **Early warning scores** such as NEWS2 identify deterioration outside the ICU and are not interchangeable with ICU mortality models.
- **Perioperative risk scores** (e.g. SORT, POSSUM) have separate inputs, case mix and intended uses.
- The choice of score must match the task.

## 12.2 APACHE II: the classic admission severity model

- **Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II)** combines the worst values of **12 physiological variables in the first 24 hours of ICU**, age and points for severe chronic organ insufficiency/immunocompromise.
- It produces a **0–71** score.
- The physiological variables are temperature, MAP, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation (PaO₂ or A–a gradient according to FiO₂), arterial pH (or bicarbonate if no ABG), sodium, potassium, creatinine (with an adjustment for acute renal failure), haematocrit, WBC and neurological state expressed as 15 minus the GCS.
- Age and chronic-health points contribute additional score.
- A higher score is generally associated with greater cohort mortality risk, but APACHE II is not a continuous instantaneous measure; it is based on a specified admission window and subsequently requires calibration/diagnostic context to convert to predicted mortality.

**Worked interpretation:**

- An 82-year-old man with septic shock, severe acidemia, MAP 55, poor oxygenation and AKI will score highly even before knowing his SOFA or response to initial treatment.
- Treating those abnormalities may substantially change his clinical trajectory, but the baseline APACHE score does not “improve” simply because he survives another day.
- Using the score to deny ICU admission would confuse risk stratification with a treatment decision.
- Chronic illness and patient priorities matter, but so do reversibility and the effect of ICU interventions.

- APACHE II limitations include population-specific calibration drift over decades, variation in how worst values are captured, bias from data missingness, effects of sedation on GCS and differences between postoperative, trauma, medical and sepsis populations.
- Later APACHE models include updated variables and require contemporary validation.
- When evaluating a scoring paper, distinguish **discrimination** (ability to rank patients; often summarised by AUROC) from **calibration** (whether predicted probabilities match observed risk) and **clinical utility** (does its use improve decisions or outcomes?).
- A high AUROC does not mean an individual probability is trustworthy.

## 12.3 Traditional SOFA: daily organ dysfunction, not an automatic diagnosis

- Traditional **Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)** assigns **0–4 points to each of six organ systems** (respiratory, coagulation, liver, cardiovascular, central nervous system and kidney), total **0–24**.
- The original criteria are built around PaO₂/FiO₂ and ventilatory support; platelets; bilirubin; MAP/vasopressor dose; GCS; and creatinine or urine output.
- A higher score indicates more severe dysfunction and higher population-level risk.
- Repeated scores show whether respiratory and cardiovascular support needs are falling while kidney function deteriorates, for example.

| **Organ** | **Traditional SOFA 0 → 4** | **Interpretation pitfall** |
|---|---|---|
| Respiratory | PaO₂/FiO₂ ≥400 (0), <400 (1), <300 (2), <200 with support (3), <100 with support (4), all in mmHg | PaO₂/FiO₂ can be influenced by FiO₂/PEEP and disease; compare context |
| Coagulation | Platelets ≥150 (0), <150 (1), <100 (2), <50 (3), <20 (4) ×10⁹/L | Bleeding, transfusion, chemotherapy and chronic thrombocytopenia can confound |
| Liver | Bilirubin <20 (0), 20–32 (1), 33–101 (2), 102–204 (3), ≥205 (4) µmol/L approximately | Cholestasis and chronic liver disease may precede the acute illness |
| Cardiovascular | MAP ≥70 and no inotrope (0); MAP <70 (1); escalating dopamine/dobutamine or noradrenaline/adrenaline (2–4) | Original vasopressor thresholds predate modern practice and vasopressin |
| CNS | GCS 15 (0), 13–14 (1), 10–12 (2), 6–9 (3), <6 (4) | Sedation and intubation confound GCS; report an assessable baseline |
| Kidney | Creatinine <110 (0), 110–170 (1), 171–299 (2), 300–440 or low urine output (3), >440 or severe oliguria (4) µmol/L approximately | Baseline CKD, fluid dilution and RRT obscure time course |

**Worked example:**

- An ICU patient has PaO₂/FiO₂ 150 mmHg on invasive ventilation (respiratory 3), platelets 90 ×10⁹/L (2), bilirubin 40 µmol/L (2), noradrenaline 0.15 µg/kg/min (traditional circulatory category 4), GCS 14 (1), creatinine 200 µmol/L (2) → a total around **14** under the original SOFA criteria.
- If their next-day vasopressor requirement drops, oxygenation improves but bilirubin rises, interpret which physiological domains changed rather than treating the single total as a sufficient explanation.
- (Note that exact traditional cardiovascular scoring depends on drug type, units and duration; use an authorised calculator.)

- SOFA was used as a component of **Sepsis-3** definitions, in which acute infection-associated SOFA increase ≥2 points represents organ dysfunction.
- Neither a high SOFA score nor a low qSOFA score is by itself a definitive diagnostic test for sepsis.
- **qSOFA** consists of altered mentation, respiratory rate ≥22/min and SBP ≤100 mmHg; it is a bedside warning tool, not a replacement for clinical suspicion or a rule-out test.

## 12.4 SOFA-2 (2025): a genuinely important update

- In October **2025**, an international group published the updated **SOFA-2** score with validation across contemporary multinational critical care datasets, including Australian and New Zealand units [R18].
- It retains six organ domains but updates thresholds, devices and vasoactive support to reflect modern ICU practice.
- For example, its respiratory categories incorporate contemporary advanced support and ECMO, the cardiovascular score uses noradrenaline/adrenaline equivalent doses and mechanical support rather than the older dopamine-based categories, and kidney scoring incorporates treatment with RRT as well as renal physiology.
- **SOFA-2 is not numerically identical to traditional SOFA**, and a score calculated using one version must not be compared uncritically with the other.

| **Domain** | **Selected SOFA-2 descriptors (2025)** | **Why new categorisation matters** |
|---|---|---|
| Brain | GCS-based categories with specified accommodations for communication, medications to treat delirium | Modern sedation and delirium can complicate neurological scoring |
| Respiration | PaO₂/FiO₂ >300 = 0; ≤300 = 1; ≤225 = 2; ≤150 with advanced support = 3; ≤75 with advanced support or ECMO = 4 | Newer oxygenation cut points and organ-support definitions |
| Cardiovascular | No pressor with MAP ≥70 = 0; MAP <70 = 1; lower → medium → higher noradrenaline/adrenaline-equivalent dose and additional agent/device = 2–4 | Avoids some historical dopamine thresholds; better captures current support |
| Liver | Bilirubin categories up to >205 µmol/L for 4 | Similar concept with updated rounding/threshold consistency |
| Kidney | Creatinine/urine-output categories and RRT included in highest category | Device support contributes explicitly rather than relying only on creatinine |
| Haemostasis | Platelet categories: >150, ≤150, ≤100, ≤80, ≤50 ×10⁹/L | Different thresholds from the original SOFA (e.g. traditional severe categories <50/<20) |

**Important exam technique:**

- State whether you are describing “traditional SOFA” or “SOFA-2”, outline the six systems, explain clinical utility and limitations, then interpret an actual patient rather than memorising every threshold without context.
- Do not retrofit new SOFA-2 platelet thresholds into a Sepsis-3 question whose original definition explicitly used traditional SOFA.

- The numerical scoring changes matter when answering a worked example.

SOFA-2 cardiovascular scoring uses the sum of noradrenaline (norepinephrine) plus adrenaline (epinephrine):

- Category 2 for ≤0.2 µg/kg/min alone (or any dose of another pressor/inotrope).
- Category 3 for >0.2–0.4 alone or ≤0.2 combined with another agent.
- Category 4 for >0.4 alone, >0.2–0.4 plus another agent, or qualifying mechanical circulatory support.

- Do not apply the traditional SOFA cut-off of noradrenaline >0.1 µg/kg/min = 4 points to the modern score.
- For example, an otherwise identical patient receiving noradrenaline 0.15 µg/kg/min may score cardiovascular 4 by traditional SOFA but cardiovascular 2 by SOFA-2 if no other agent or device is present.
- This difference is a change in scale, not necessarily improvement in the patient [R18].

- Other SOFA-2 thresholds are similarly updated: respiratory PaO₂/FiO₂ >300 = 0, ≤300 = 1, ≤225 = 2, ≤150 with advanced ventilatory support = 3, and ≤75 with advanced support or ECMO = 4. The platelet thresholds are >150, ≤150, ≤100, ≤80 and ≤50 ×10⁹/L for scores 0–4, whereas traditional SOFA uses ≥150, <150, <100, <50 and <20 ×10⁹/L.
- SOFA-2 renal scoring can allocate 4 points to patients receiving or fulfilling criteria for KRT; this is both an important clinical descriptor and a confounder when comparing treatment strategies.
- Always state the version and units, account for confounders such as sedation/neurological assessment and treatment limitation, and avoid converting a score to an individual mortality prediction without a validated model.

## 12.5 What a good candidate says when asked to evaluate severity scores

A concise critical appraisal considers:

- Intended population, prediction horizon and inputs.
- Discrimination and calibration.
- Internal and external validation.
- Missing-data handling and bias.
- Whether reassessment or case-mix adjustment is appropriate.
- Whether the score changes management.

- Population averages must not determine ceilings of treatment on their own.
- Scores can facilitate risk-adjusted audit, ICU benchmarking, resource planning and communication, yet they may also amplify inequity if they encode historical access to treatment, comorbidity or treatment limitations.
- Be particularly cautious with patients with disabilities, chronic organ dysfunction, altered baseline function or a different case mix from the derivation population.

items.title: 13. Prolonged ICU admission: complications, prevention and recovery
items.body:
## 13.1 Why survival and functional recovery are not the same outcome

- Advances in organ support mean that patients survive illnesses previously considered fatal, but prolonged ICU treatment can leave cognitive, physical, psychological and social sequelae.
- The umbrella term **post-intensive care syndrome (PICS)** describes new or worsened impairments in physical function, cognition and mental health after critical illness.
- It can coexist with persistent underlying disease and pre-existing frailty.
- Family members may develop anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance and PTSD (**PICS-F**).
- The purpose of an ICU survivorship approach is therefore not simply to shorten length of stay, but to support recovery of function, autonomy and quality of life.

## 13.2 ICU-acquired weakness (ICUAW)

- ICUAW includes **critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP)**, **critical illness myopathy (CIM)** and overlapping disorders.
- CIP is an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy associated with severe inflammation and microvascular dysfunction; CIM reflects alterations in muscle membrane excitability and contractile proteins, worsened by catabolism and immobility.
- Patients develop symmetric, usually flaccid weakness, difficult ventilator liberation, poor cough and reduced mobility.
- Cranial nerve muscles may be relatively spared in classical patterns, but coexisting neurological disease can alter presentation.
- Risk factors include sepsis, multiorgan failure, hyperglycaemia, immobility, prolonged ventilation and certain pharmacological exposures; neuromuscular blockade itself is not the sole explanation.

- **Diagnosis** begins with a bedside examination in an awake cooperative patient: the Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score tests six bilateral muscle groups (maximum 60); a score **<48/60** supports clinically significant ICU-acquired weakness.
- The assessment may be impossible during delirium, deep sedation or cognitive impairment.
- Reflexes, sensation and nerve-conduction/electromyography can distinguish neuropathic and myopathic components when clinically useful.
- Exclude other causes such as Guillain–Barré syndrome, spinal cord injury, electrolyte depletion, steroid myopathy, residual paralysis and focal nerve lesions.
- Treatment is supportive: mobilise early when stable, optimise nutrition and glycaemia, avoid avoidable deep sedation, treat sepsis and support progressive rehabilitation.
- There is no established drug that reverses ICUAW quickly.

## 13.3 Long-term organ, cognitive and psychological complications

| **Domain** | **Typical problems** | **Assessment and prevention/recovery strategy** |
|---|---|---|
| Respiratory | Prolonged weaning, tracheostomy dependence, diaphragmatic dysfunction, reduced exercise tolerance | Daily respiratory/airway review, SBTs, secretion/cough assessment, physiotherapy and pulmonary rehab |
| Renal/cardiovascular | Persistent AKI/CKD, hypertension, myocardial dysfunction, thromboembolism | Serial creatinine, fluid/electrolyte assessment, thromboprophylaxis, cardiology/renal follow-up as indicated |
| Musculoskeletal | ICUAW, contractures, pressure injury, critical illness bone loss | Early mobilisation, positioning/splinting, pain control, physiotherapy/OT, nutrition and skin care |
| Neurocognitive | Impaired attention, memory, executive function, sleep and communication | Delirium prevention, cognitive screening, meaningful rehabilitation, sleep/circadian restoration |
| Psychological | Anxiety, depression, PTSD, delusional ICU memories, loss of confidence | Explain events, involve family, ICU diary where appropriate, psychological follow-up and support |
| Nutrition/GI | Sarcopenia, dysphagia after intubation, poor appetite, micronutrient deficiencies | Dietitian and speech-language review, swallow assessment, adequate nutrition and gradual exercise |
| Social/family | Loss of work, financial strain, caregiver burden, change in relationships | Social work, supported discharge, rehabilitation planning, family review and referral |

The complications interact: deep sedation promotes immobility, delirium and delayed extubation; prolonged ventilation contributes to dysphagia and weakness; untreated pain impairs sleep and mobilisation; malnutrition limits rehab. A long-stay review should therefore include all domains rather than “daily physiology plus discharge planning.”

## 13.4 Prevention begins early in ICU

- After stabilising the initial illness, use minimised sedation, daily SBT/SAT coordination, mobilisation within physiological limits, adequate pain management, delirium screening, sleep preservation, line/device review, pressure-area care, VTE prevention, family engagement and a realistic rehabilitation plan.
- Early physiotherapy may require short sessions and stepwise progression (passive → active exercises → sitting → standing → assisted walking) rather than aggressive rehabilitation during escalating shock or severe hypoxaemia.
- Later, give a coherent discharge summary that records ICU complications, delirium, organ injuries, medications requiring taper, nutritional needs, mobility, cognitive concerns and arranged follow-up.

- A prolonged ICU patient needs an organised weekly functional assessment alongside daily organ physiology.
- Document current muscle strength and mobilisation level, delirium/cognitive state, pain and opioid exposure, sleep, nutrition intake versus targets, swallowing/voice and tracheostomy status, pressure injury, VTE risk, bowel/bladder function, hearing/vision aids, family concerns and rehabilitation goals.
- New weakness should trigger examination for focal neurological injury, myopathy, neuropathy, phosphate depletion and residual blockade rather than automatically being called deconditioning.
- Dysphagia after prolonged intubation carries aspiration risk, and a speech-language therapist assessment may be required before oral feeding or decannulation.

- The discharge pathway is a physiological intervention: avoid unplanned abrupt cessation of opioid/benzodiazepine therapy, confirm equipment and oxygen needs, arrange renal/cardiac/pulmonary follow-up where injury persists, and provide the patient and family with an understandable account of the ICU illness, delirium and expected recovery trajectory.
- Some survivors need cognitive rehabilitation, psychological treatment or return-to-work support.
- PICS-F can include clinically important anxiety, depression and traumatic stress in whānau/caregivers.
- These domains are not captured by APACHE or discharge creatinine and are central to evaluating ICU care beyond survival.

**PICS should also change how we discuss risk at ICU admission.** A patient may survive a prolonged stay but not return to their pre-illness level of independence; this uncertainty needs sensitive discussion without assuming that a life with disability has little value. Rehabilitation goals should be set with the patient whenever possible and revisited during recovery.

items.title: 14. Setting therapeutic goals for ICU admission and treatment
items.body:
## 14.1 Why ICU admission is a treatment decision, not just a location

- An ICU bed offers advanced observation, organ support and expertise but imposes treatment burdens: invasive lines, ventilation, medications, delirium, separation, loss of autonomy and sometimes prolonged dependency.
- The purpose of admission is to provide **proportionate treatment that offers a reasonable chance of achieving goals important to the patient**.
- Potential benefit depends on the acuity and reversibility of illness, likely response to available interventions, burden of treatment, premorbid function and the patient’s informed preferences.
- Admission must not be decided by age, disability, diagnosis or a scoring threshold alone.

- An early discussion should clarify the working diagnosis, which organ functions are failing, whether short-term organ support can reverse the problem, and what a successful outcome would mean to this individual.
- For example, a previously independent patient with severe but reversible pneumonia may reasonably undergo ventilation and vasopressors; a patient with irreversible terminal disease may prefer comfort-oriented care without burdensome organ support.
- The patient may also value a **time-limited trial of ICU** with predefined reassessment points rather than unconditional or immediate refusal of therapy.

## 14.2 Goals of care versus “for resuscitation” labels

- A **goals-of-care plan** identifies values and desired outcomes and can guide ceilings of treatment (e.g. intubation, dialysis, CPR) in context.
- A **treatment-limitation order** specifies particular interventions considered inappropriate or not wanted.
- A **DNACPR** order applies to cardiopulmonary resuscitation after arrest and does not automatically mean no antibiotics, surgery, oxygen, analgesia or admission.
- Likewise, “full treatment” should not be interpreted as an instruction to continue physiologically ineffective interventions forever.
- The clinician must understand the document’s scope, consent/advance-directive legal status, current circumstances and patient preferences.

- Decisions require communication with the patient if they have capacity, or legally appropriate substitute/representative processes where they lack it, using applicable New Zealand or Australian law and hospital policy.
- Family are indispensable in understanding the patient’s values and in shared communication, but may not always be the formal decision-maker.
- Cultural safety is particularly important: ask whether the person wants whānau/family, cultural or spiritual support involved, and avoid assuming a single decision-making model.
- Include nursing and allied health perspectives and a senior ICU review for high-stakes decisions.

## 14.3 Time-limited trials and reassessment

- A time-limited trial may be ethically useful when prognosis is uncertain and a reversible process is possible.
- Before starting, document the proposed support (e.g. ventilation, vasopressors, antimicrobial/source control), which outcomes will be assessed (improvement in shock, oxygenation, renal recovery, neurological findings), a review interval, patient-valued outcomes and what will happen if there is no improvement.
- **Do not promise that a fixed trial duration can determine prognosis reliably**; the review is a structured conversation, not an automatic stop date.
- If irreversible multiorgan failure develops despite appropriate treatment, reassess burdens, benefit and whether continued support remains consistent with goals.

- Withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment is ethically and clinically distinct from abandonment.
- Comfort care is **active treatment** of pain, dyspnoea, anxiety, nausea, agitation and distress.
- Anticipate symptoms when withdrawing ventilation or vasopressors, maintain communication and dignity, and document the plan and rationale.
- Seek senior, ethics or palliative support in disagreement or uncertainty.
- Analgesics and sedatives are titrated to relieve symptoms, not to deliberately hasten death.
- Consider tissue/organ donation conversations separately and sensitively when relevant; donation is not an automatic consequence of treatment withdrawal.

- A specialist should be able to describe how a time-limited trial is implemented.
- Suppose an older patient with previously independent function has aspiration pneumonia, severe hypoxaemia and uncertain reversibility.
- Explain the proposed interventions (ventilation, antibiotics, fluids/vasopressors as appropriate), the expected burdens (delirium, invasive procedures, immobility) and the outcomes that will be reviewed (improvement in oxygenation and vasopressor dose, microbiology/source control, ability to lighten sedation, emerging organ failure and the person's own acceptable future function).
- Document who has decision-making capacity, the relevant advance-care plan, the nominated legally recognised representative if applicable and the reassessment interval.
- A deteriorating APACHE/SOFA score contributes context but never determines the ceiling of care alone.

- When a transition to comfort-focused care becomes appropriate, use a positive symptom plan: treat dyspnoea, pain, agitation and secretions, consider anticipatory opioid and anxiolytic prescriptions according to local palliative guidance, organise a family meeting, explain the likely physiological course, and reassess comfort after withdrawal of support.
- DNACPR is not equivalent to withdrawal of antibiotics or to the absence of all ICU care.
- Decisions are informed by New Zealand or Australian law and current local policy; ethical justification rests on patient values, proportionality, likely benefit, consent and fair access, rather than age or diagnosis in isolation.

## 14.4 Scarce resources and escalation in practice

- When ICU capacity is limited, fair triage must rely on transparent, consistent institutional processes focused on potential clinical benefit and proportionality, not informal assumptions about a patient’s worth.
- Consider whether the required intervention can be safely provided elsewhere, whether transfer is appropriate and what risk it creates.
- Document changes in patient condition and the rationale for decisions; review frequently because benefit, bed capacity and available services can change.
- Evidence-based severity scores can aid audit but **should not be the sole criterion to admit, refuse, limit or withdraw ICU**.

items.title: 15. Personnel, equipment and drugs for crisis management in anaesthetising locations
items.body:
## 15.1 Preparation is itself a patient-safety intervention

- A crisis plan is most effective when its personnel, locations, equipment and drugs are known before the event.
- Operating theatres, procedure rooms, cath labs, imaging suites, obstetric theatres, endoscopy and ICU all differ in immediate access to an anaesthesia machine, emergency airway equipment, defibrillator, blood and experienced help.
- The learning outcome is not satisfied by saying “call for help and use the emergency trolley”; a specialist should be able to locate resources, allocate tasks and coordinate escalation for the specific site.

- At the beginning of a list or high-risk case verify: oxygen supply and backup, suction, a tested breathing system and ventilator, monitoring (ECG/SpO₂/NIBP/ETCO₂; temperature when needed), functioning resuscitation/defibrillation equipment, an airway rescue plan including front-of-neck access, and access to emergency drugs and blood.
- In a remote location, consider the time to obtain help, the route to ICU/theatre, and whether the team can maintain ventilation and perfusion during transfer.

## 15.2 Who should respond and what they do

**Team leader:**

- Maintains global overview, prioritises interventions and allocates roles; one team member can lead initially but senior anaesthetic/ICU leadership should be summoned.
- **Airway operator:** ventilates, checks capnography and prepares rescue airway.
- **Compressor/defibrillator operator:** provides CPR and shocks with minimum pauses.
- **Drug/vascular-access clinician:** administers time-critical therapy and confirms preparation, route, dose and flush.
- **Recorder/timekeeper:** records arrest time, rhythms, shocks, adrenaline cycles and key decisions, and prompts rhythm checks.
- **Runner:** obtains blood, specialised drugs, ultrasound, equipment or another team.
- **Surgical/procedural operator:** ceases causative stimulus and provides definitive source control or access.
- **Nurse coordinator:** prepares infusions, monitors, assists circulation and liaises with blood bank/ICU.

- Closed-loop communication avoids omissions: “Adrenaline 1 mg IV now” → “I am giving adrenaline 1 mg IV” → “Adrenaline 1 mg IV given at 14:03.” The leader requests focused updates (“current rhythm, ETCO₂, likely cause, next shock?”), rather than allowing simultaneous conversations.
- Cognitive aids support attention under stress but require familiarity, readable placement and practice.

## 15.3 A practical resource inventory

| **Emergency** | **Equipment and access** | **Drugs/blood and special resources** |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiac/respiratory arrest | Defibrillator and pads, bag–mask, suction, oxygen, ETTs, SGAs, video/direct laryngoscope, waveform CO₂, IV/IO access, arterial line/echo when available | Adrenaline 1:10,000, amiodarone or lignocaine, saline flush, calcium for specific indications; resuscitation algorithm |
| Failed airway/CICO | Airway trolley, flexible scope/video laryngoscope, second-generation SGA, front-of-neck access kit, oxygenation devices | Prepared oxygen/induction or rescue drugs; trained surgical/anaesthetic help; difficult-airway cognitive aid |
| Major haemorrhage | Rapid infuser, warming devices, large-bore cannulae, blood tubing, laboratory/POC VHA as available | Emergency red cells, major haemorrhage protocol packs, TXA where indicated, fibrinogen/platelets/plasma, calcium, cell salvage if suitable |
| Anaphylaxis | Airway/ventilation, fluids, infusion pumps, arterial pressure if time permits | Correct adrenaline concentration, crystalloid, bronchodilator, anaphylaxis algorithm, tryptase sampling plan |
| Malignant hyperthermia | Volatile-free circuit/activated charcoal filters if stocked, cooling resources, temperature monitoring | Dantrolene sufficient for immediate treatment and additional stock, sterile diluent, MH algorithm, blood gases/electrolytes |
| LAST | CPR/airway, ultrasound/rescue support and appropriate monitoring | **20% lipid emulsion** with dosing aid, benzodiazepine, access to prolonged mechanical support |
| Severe obstetric emergency | Obstetric and neonatal teams, airway, theatre and surgical delivery capability | Uterotonics, massive haemorrhage resources, magnesium sulfate/calcium rescue as appropriate, obstetric algorithms |
| Remote anaesthetic location | Transport monitor, battery backup, portable ventilator/oxygen cylinder, infusion continuity, secure lines and access | Site-specific emergency drugs, portable suction, communications, retrieval/ICU escalation plan |

- Check **expiry, concentrations and quantities** rather than assuming a named drug exists in the right form.
- High-alert medications—including concentrated adrenaline, potassium, neuromuscular blockers and local anaesthetics—need clear labelling, independent cross-checks where feasible and a standardised location.
- A malignant hyperthermia stock policy is only useful if dantrolene can actually reach a theatre rapidly; a defibrillator is useful only if pads, batteries, access and staff competence exist.
- Local emergency-management training and simulation should test equipment retrieval as well as clinical knowledge.

- A realistic crisis-resource check drills down from the name of a trolley to the practical ability to treat an immediately life-threatening event.
- For a remote anaesthesia location, identify where the defibrillator is kept and whether pads for the patient's size are available, who can provide hands-free compressions, who brings the difficult-airway and front-of-neck access kit, where emergency blood is issued, how quickly local anaesthetic lipid rescue or dantrolene can arrive, and whether the gas supply has a functional backup.
- Confirm the anticipated rescue drugs are present in usable concentrations: for example, diluted arrest adrenaline 1 mg/10 mL is not interchangeable with 1 mg/mL ampoules for titrated non-arrest boluses.
- Deliberately separate and label calcium chloride, potassium-containing concentrates, tranexamic acid and neuromuscular blockers to limit look-alike/sound-alike errors.

- The team leader should state an escalation plan before a high-risk case: triggers for calling another anaesthetist, surgical control of bleeding, activation of the major-haemorrhage protocol, escalation to ICU/cardiac surgery, and who coordinates retrieval of unavailable equipment.
- Cognitive aids must be physically accessible, readable, tested and integrated into simulation.
- After a crisis, incident review should ask whether key equipment arrived on time, whether the drug preparation was correct, whether the handover captured reversible causes and what must change in the system; the goal is safer future care, not merely a retrospective knowledge quiz.

## 15.4 Debriefing and learning after the event

- After immediate stabilisation and patient/family communication, conduct a short factual hot debrief when feasible: what happened, what went well, what was difficult and what needs prompt correction.
- Preserve the clinical record, report relevant incidents, arrange staff support and a more structured review or root-cause investigation for significant events.
- The aim is system learning—workload, human factors, equipment, escalation, communication, cognitive aids—not automatic attribution of individual blame.
- Treat psychological safety and confidential process requirements seriously.

items.title: 16. Worked integrated ANZCA Final cases
items.los: Integrates the outcomes in this set
items.body:
## Case 1 — A shockable intraoperative arrest during major abdominal surgery

A 68-year-old undergoes laparotomy, develops marked ST depression and falls from MAP 75 to 35 mmHg. ETCO₂ falls from 35 to 12 mmHg, then the arterial trace disappears and VF appears on ECG.

**Reasoned approach:**

- Recognise absent perfusing arterial trace and VF, announce arrest, 100% O₂, initiate compressions, charge/defibrillate promptly with appropriate biphasic energy, immediately resume CPR, and use the rhythm-specific sequence (adrenaline after second unsuccessful shock, amiodarone after third).
- Simultaneously exclude rapidly correctable mechanical/drug causes (haemorrhage, hypoxaemia, potassium disturbance, surgical manipulation) while treating suspected myocardial ischaemia.
- After ROSC: ABG, echo, ECG, MAP/oxygen/ventilation optimisation and coronary investigation; serial troponin alone is not diagnostic of culprit occlusion.
- Consider post-arrest myocardial stunning even when the initial trigger was coronary ischaemia.

## Case 2 — Post-cardiac-surgery PEA on the ICU monitor

A patient six hours after CABG abruptly becomes hypotensive, followed by loss of arterial pulsatility; ECG shows a paced rhythm, chest drains have stopped unexpectedly, and the team suspects tamponade.

**Reasoned approach:**

- Activate CALS–ANZ; check pacing/underlying rhythm including occult VF, rapidly summon cardiac surgery, prepare emergency re-sternotomy within five minutes and manage airway, perfusion and reversible causes.
- A short initial interruption to ordinary compressions may permit targeted pacing/stacked shocks, but do not omit compressions during continued preparation.
- In tamponade, reopening the chest and clearing clot corrects the mechanism; more adrenaline without decompression is unlikely to solve the problem.

## Case 3 — Unresponsive after ROSC, temperature 38.2°C

After 12 minutes of resuscitation, a patient regains circulation but remains comatose on propofol, noradrenaline and invasive ventilation. PaO₂ is 250 mmHg on FiO₂ 1.0; PaCO₂ 29 mmHg; temperature 38.2°C.

**Reasoned approach:**

- Titrate FiO₂ to a monitored normoxic target (ANZCOR SpO₂ 94–98%), correct hypocapnia towards normocapnia, initiate active fever prevention to ≤37.5°C for at least 72 hours, treat ongoing shock according to echo and perfusion, and seek the arrest cause.
- Do not pronounce a poor neurological prognosis from the current examination under sedation; plan delayed multimodal assessment when confounders resolve.

## Case 4 — The apparently agitated ventilated patient

A patient on postoperative day 4 is thrashing on a ventilator despite propofol 3 mg/kg/h. CPOT 6, RASS +2 and a large volume of urine is retained in the bladder; abdominal wound is tender.

**Reasoned approach:**

- Agitation may be pain and retention, not sedative failure.
- Check ventilator, gases, oxygenation, catheter and haemodynamics; address urinary retention and provide appropriate analgesia/regionally targeted relief; then reassess CPOT and RASS.
- If distress persists, screen for delirium and withdrawal before escalating sedation.
- Deepening propofol without examining the patient could cause unnecessary hypotension and mask a reversible problem.

## Case 5 — Suspected propofol infusion syndrome

A 43-year-old with sepsis has received a high-dose propofol infusion for several days and develops a new pH 7.12, lactate 9 mmol/L, CK 8,000 U/L, potassium 6.4 mmol/L, widening QRS and increasing noradrenaline requirement.

**Reasoned approach:**

- Treat all causes of shock and ischaemia, but explicitly suspect PRIS from the combination of high-dose/prolonged propofol, unexplained acidaemia, rhabdomyolysis and cardiac dysfunction.
- Stop propofol immediately, provide another sedative, stabilise hyperkalaemia, support circulation, investigate renal and cardiac injury and consider CRRT or mechanical support.
- Do not wait for a confirmatory “PRIS test”; none exists.

## Case 6 — Risk of refeeding after a long ICU course

A previously malnourished patient with significant weight loss has had minimal nutrition for nine days. On restarting an enteral feed, phosphate falls from 0.85 to 0.38 mmol/L, with falling magnesium and new ventilatory weakness.

**Reasoned approach:**

- This is high-risk refeeding syndrome physiology.
- Reduce delivered energy substantially for a monitored period, provide thiamine, replace phosphate/magnesium/potassium according to renal status and local guidance, review fluid balance and glucose, monitor electrolytes at least 12-hourly or more frequently if unstable, and advance feeds slowly after stabilisation.
- Do not simply switch EN to PN: both routes can drive the insulin response.

## Case 7 — The SOFA score is rising but the ventilator is improving

A patient with sepsis becomes less oxygen-dependent but now needs haemofiltration, has rising bilirubin and a falling platelet count. The team describes “respiratory recovery” while total organ dysfunction worsens.

- **Reasoned approach:** report each SOFA domain and version (traditional versus SOFA-2), demonstrate the direction of change, search for new liver, renal or coagulation insults and review therapy-related complications. An improved PaO₂/FiO₂ is not a global improvement, and no score substitutes for the clinical mechanism or patient-centred goals discussion.

## Case 8 — A time-limited trial of ICU and uncertain long-term outcome

A frail patient with severe pneumonia has a reasonable chance of short-term improvement but fears prolonged invasive ventilation and loss of independence. Family members disagree about intubation.

**Reasoned approach:**

- Evaluate capacity and seek the patient’s values and advance preferences, explain plausible outcomes and treatment burdens, discuss a documented time-limited trial with defined treatments and reassessment criteria, involve senior ICU and appropriate support, and distinguish a DNACPR order from other treatments.
- Avoid using frailty or age alone as a veto, or promising that ventilator liberation necessarily means a return to baseline quality of life.

## Case 9 — Adult versus term-newborn ALS (cross-curriculum distinction)

- **Adult cardiac arrest** is commonly a primary arrhythmic/cardiac or sudden circulatory event: initiate CPR, rapidly distinguish shockable from non-shockable rhythm, defibrillate VF/pVT, use compressions ≈100–120/min with 30:2 until advanced airway and 1 mg adrenaline according to rhythm sequence.
- In a **newly born term infant**, compromise is most commonly **asphyxial** and the key first intervention is **effective positive-pressure ventilation** when apnoeic/gasping or heart rate <100/min; begin coordinated **3:1 compression-to-ventilation** (90 compressions and 30 breaths/min) if HR remains **<60/min despite ≥30 seconds of effective ventilation**, using two-thumb technique at one-third AP chest depth.
- If HR remains <60 despite effective ventilation and compressions, use **IV adrenaline 10–30 µg/kg** via umbilical access where feasible and repeat every 3–5 minutes as indicated.
- This is not a “small adult” dose or rhythm-first algorithm.
- The reasons are neonatal transitional physiology, rate-dependent cardiac output and the primacy of hypoxic respiratory failure [R19].

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
- A specialist should know the difference between **evidence supporting an intervention’s mechanism**, **evidence of improved intermediate physiological endpoints** and **evidence of improved patient-centred outcomes**.
- Several treatments in intensive care have excellent physiological rationale yet neutral effects on survival when tested in large trials.
- The table below deliberately distinguishes positive, neutral and uncertain findings; the source links are in §20.

| **Trial / year** | **Question and principal finding** | **Practical interpretation** |
|---|---|---|
| **PARAMEDIC2 (2018)** | Adrenaline in out-of-hospital arrest increased 30-day survival **3.2% versus 2.4%**, but did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in favourable neurological outcome | Continue evidence-based adrenaline in ALS, but recognise ROSC and neurological recovery are different outcomes; extrapolation to witnessed perioperative arrest is limited [R26] |
| **TTM2 (2021)** | Target 33°C versus active normothermia/fever management after OHCA: no benefit in 6-month mortality or functional outcome; more arrhythmia with hypothermia | Consistent active fever prevention is essential; routine induction to 33°C is not proven superior for all patients [R07] |
| **Kress et al. (2000)** | Daily interruption of sedative infusions shortened ventilation duration in a small RCT | Established protocolised wake-up as an alternative to unexamined continuous deep sedation; modern practice pursues light sedation even without mandatory interruption [R25] |
| **SPICE III (2019)** | Early dexmedetomidine versus usual sedation: 90-day mortality **29.1% in each arm**; bradycardia/hypotension more frequent with dexmedetomidine | Do not claim mortality benefit from routine early dexmedetomidine [R09] |
| **MENDS2 (2021)** | Dexmedetomidine versus propofol in sepsis: no difference in days alive without delirium/coma or 90-day survival | Neither agent is universally superior; sedation depth and non-drug care remain crucial [R10] |
| **NONSEDA (2020)** | No-sedation strategy versus light sedation/daily interruption: no significant 90-day mortality improvement | Lack of sedation is not a universally better goal; prioritise comfort and patient safety with the lowest appropriate drug burden [R11] |
| **EPaNIC (2011)** | Early versus delayed supplemental PN: delayed group had fewer infections, faster recovery, similar mortality | Avoid routine early supplemental PN simply to achieve full calculated targets [R14] |
| **TARGET (2018)** | Higher-calorie 1.5 kcal/mL EN versus routine 1.0 kcal/mL: no improvement in 90-day mortality | Higher early calorie delivery is not automatically advantageous [R15] |
| **NUTRIREA-3 (2023)** | Low early energy/protein vs standard during vasopressor-dependent shock: no significant mortality difference; fewer GI events in low-intake arm | Start/advance cautiously in unstable shock; do not overfeed in acute phase [R16] |
| **EFFORT Protein (2023)** | ≥2.2 g/kg/day prescribed protein did not improve discharge alive versus usual ≤1.2 g/kg/day; possible harm in AKI/high-severity subgroups | Avoid universal very-high-dose early protein [R13] |
| **SOFA-2 validation (2025)** | International derivation/validation of revised organ-dysfunction descriptors and thresholds | Use and identify score version; do not compare original and SOFA-2 totals indiscriminately [R18] |

## 17.1 How to answer an examiner’s “critically evaluate” prompt

- For arrest, first state what improves survival mechanistically (early recognition, no-flow minimisation, compressions, defibrillation, reversal of cause), then discuss the limitations of adrenaline, airway devices, mechanical CPR, antiarrhythmics and neuroprognostication evidence.
- For sedation, distinguish reduced delirium prevalence from mortality benefit and explain drug trade-offs.
- For nutritional support, describe risk from both underfeeding and overfeeding, the difference between early shock and recovery phases, and why three landmark trials do not support forcing full energy/protein targets immediately.
- For severity scoring, include **discrimination, calibration, case mix and the danger of treating a score as a patient-level prognosis**.

- The minimum critical-appraisal standard is to state the trial's population, intervention, comparator, primary patient-centred outcome and whether the result applies to your actual patient.
- For PARAMEDIC2 and AIRWAYS-2, both randomised out-of-hospital arrests: interpret the small absolute outcome differences and acknowledge the major difference from a rapidly witnessed perioperative arrest.
- For INCEPTION, consider selection to shockable refractory out-of-hospital arrest and transfer/cannulation times rather than generalising ECPR to all ICU arrests.
- For TTM2, the comparison is active fever prevention versus routine 33°C cooling—not cooling versus abandoning temperature care.
- For EPaNIC, TARGET, NUTRIREA-3 and EFFORT Protein, delivery strategy, shock severity, nutritional risk and timing all matter: no one study proves that prolonged underfeeding is safe or that higher protein is always harmful.
- This comparison is central to an ANZCA Final “critically evaluate” question and is as important as remembering numerical results.

items.body:
## Evidence audit and scope

The chapters were written first, then checked separately against the exact Set 9 assignments below. The outcome text is copied from the uploaded **Prioritised LEarning Sets(4).xlsx**, sheet **09 ICU Integration**, rather than retrospectively taken from another teaching document. In particular, the full IT_RT 1.2 parent outcome extends across numerous emergencies; **only its cardiac-arrest component is assigned to Set 9**, so the parent LO must not be marked fully complete here.

### 18.2 Independent depth and clinical correctness audit

**Arrest and perioperative emergencies (IT_RT 1.2 component, AT_RT 2.5a, SS_IC 1.40):** Checked recognition, aetiological classification, early monitored physiological clues, high-quality CPR, rhythm-specific shocks and drugs, reversible causes, perioperative exceptions, CALS–ANZ, pregnancy, post-ROSC care, neurological prognosis and resuscitation goals. Confirmed ANZCOR **after-second-shock adrenaline**, **after-third-shock amiodarone**, **200 J default biphasic**, appropriate 2-minute cycles, and **2026 special-circumstances** distinctions. The neonatal contrast is supplemental examiner-relevant application, not a claim that full newborn resuscitation outcomes are completed in Set 9.

**Analgesia/sedation and pharmacology (SS_IC 1.4, 1.5 and 1.6):** Checked analgesia-first strategy, CPOT/BPS/RASS/CAM-ICU interpretation, ventilator and neurological conditions needing deeper sedation, non-pharmacological delirium prevention, relative advantages/limitations of major drugs, withdrawal physiology and tapering, propofol infusion syndrome and latest PADIS conditional recommendation. Drug ranges are deliberately described as typical starting contexts rather than universal prescriptions.

**Metabolism and nutrition (SS_IC 1.2, 1.3 and 1.74):** Checked stress hormone/cytokine physiology; feed timing, route, energy/protein estimation, propofol calories, gastrointestinal intolerance, vasopressor-dependent shock, PN risks, refeeding prevention and treatment, and genuine trial results rather than only trial names. Special diets, obesity, RRT and prolonged rehabilitation require individualised plans rather than a single fixed target.

**Scoring, long-stay ICU and goals of care (SS_IC 1.10, 1.11, 1.1):** Checked APACHE II variable domains, limitations, original SOFA versus SOFA-2 (2025), how to interpret organ-specific trends, PICS/ICUAW diagnosis and prevention, patient-centred goals, time-limited trials, ethical limitations and the distinction between DNACPR and full treatment withdrawal. The MRC sum score and appropriate delirium/rehabilitation tools are explained in their clinical context.

**Crisis resources (IT_RT 1.3):** Checked physical resources, their locations/roles, team coordination, critical drug availability, airway/blood/defibrillator/access requirements, site-specific planning, closed-loop communication and post-event debrief. Knowing a resource list is not equivalent to equipment competence; teams must verify availability and practise retrieval and use.

### 18.3 Why some neighbouring content is intentionally not duplicated

The workbook places comprehensive mechanical ventilation, sepsis management, metabolic electrolyte crises, neurocritical care, transfusion and cardiac disease in Sets 1–8, 10–13 and beyond. Set 9 uses those mechanisms to teach **integrated ICU decisions**; it does not replicate every drug or procedure in other sets. Similarly, historical SAQ model answers with examiner marking schedules are a separate output: the examination reports inform these teaching chapters, but they cannot establish that every SAQ since 2006 is reproduced here.

**Source limitation:** The available project examiner reports span selected sittings in 2015–2026 and the workbook has a broader historical mapping. Proprietary textbook chapters and all individual Blue Book issue chapters have not been independently verified in full. Specific recommendations are grounded primarily in accessible contemporary professional guidelines and primary trials; the reading list below identifies verifiable BJA Education and Blue Book material without attributing unverified claims to them.

Audit judgement after amendment (November 2026): all 13 assigned Set 9 parent rows have been individually matched to their intended clinical component. The twelve marked “complete in Set 9” are taught in the corresponding chapters; IT_RT 1.2 remains a partial cardiac-arrest component, and no claim is made to completing its other emergencies. The audit specifically rechecked high-stakes dose/timing pathways against ANZCOR 11.2/11.7/11.8/11.10; PADIS's conditional, context-dependent dexmedetomidine recommendation; current nutrition evidence including EFFORT Protein and NUTRIREA-3; the original SOFA and the actual SOFA-2 scoring table; NICE/ASPEN refeeding definitions and risk criteria; and the relevant uploaded examiner reports. Important areas not verified against proprietary textbook full text are declared as source limitations rather than inferred coverage. Practical proficiency in CALS, front-of-neck access, ultrasound and emergency equipment retrieval cannot be established by written notes alone.

## Recommended reading

- **1.** **Jabaudon & Constantin (2024),** [Sedation with volatile anaesthetics in intensive care](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.12.004)**, BJA Education.** Useful for the different pharmacokinetics, hardware, exposure and clinical limitations of inhaled ICU sedation; adjunct rather than a replacement for the PADIS guidance.
- **2.** **Boncyk et al. (2024),** [Management of pain and sedation in the intensive care unit](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-079789)**, BMJ.** Full conceptual framework for analgesia-first care, light sedation, patient experience and clinical trial evidence.
- **3.** **Bergbower & Bechek (2026),** [Sedation and analgesia in the critically ill](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bpa.2026.07.003)**, Best Practice & Research Clinical Anaesthesiology.** Newer synthesis of the practical sedation literature.
